中国村落的特征
中文

第三节 中国村落的特征

人们定居下来以后，为了生存，必然会在一定的范围内进行生产生活和繁衍，在生产生活的过程中不断积累相关的经验，耕种以谋生，建房以居住，交流以相处。日积月累，不断发展，于是生发出相应的文化。概而言之，所谓传统村落文化的范畴，即是指在传统农耕社会中，人们在群居的基础上进行的系列生产生活的过程中所形成的一切物质文化和非物质文化的总和。也就是说，传统村落文化不仅包括有形的建筑文化，而且应该包括生活在传统村落中的"人"，以及由"人"所创造、传承的一切有形的和无形的文化形态。

有形的显性的文化形态，大多体现在传统建筑中，甚至隐性的文化也有在建筑中予以体现和反映的。以长江中游的湖南地方为例，如湘中的府第式建筑，往往是以一家人或一个家族为一个整体的大院落，其建筑从空间布局到功能体现忠实地遵循着传统汉文化的礼乐秩序，甚至制度文化意义重于实际居住功能的需求。如双峰曾国藩的家府，就是儒家居住等级与制度文化的典范。"中为堂，左为尊，右为次"，"东阶为主，西厢待客"，没有丝毫的僭越或者疏忽，可谓"秩序井然"。

而湘南地区郴州一带聚族而居的村落，往往是一栋栋独立的住宅，此接彼连，整体上形成气势恢宏的村落。虽然每一个住宅同样体现了礼乐秩序的传统精神，但从大的格局来看，单个住宅之间既相对独立，又维系在一个族群的大框架系统之中，与祠堂等公共建筑相匹配，在"慎终追远""长幼有序、尊卑有别"的儒家伦理文化的基本体系之下，独立的空间布局便于营造出相对宽松的人际关系和生存理念，个体的主观独立愿望在客观的空间布局中基本可以得到尊重，与湘中的大宅院把个体（人）完全淹没于隐性的制度文化之中形成明显差别。

这种差别，不仅仅体现在建筑文化上，也反映在建筑的壁画上，湘中和湘南呈现出两种完全不同的基调。湘中府第式庄园建筑上的壁画，多能见到以人伦秩序教化为主题内容的庄重严肃的题材，如同家训，成教化、助人伦的劝诱功能已超出了作为绘画艺术自身应当具备的审美愉悦。即便是应当使人轻松的戏剧题材，也蒙上了些许沉郁的威仪。而在湘南，富有个性化的艺术表达则非常突出和典型。正襟危坐的家训式场景描绘很少见，而纯粹欣赏性的山水楼台、花鸟人物和雅士偏好的松、竹、梅、兰题材则成为主流。

从绘画的技法看，湘中地区的壁画技法讲究规整严谨，无一不呈现出正统文化的气息，令观者不由得端正严肃、敬而畏之。湘南地区的壁画则并无太多的技法讲究和制约，笔随意走、画由兴出，所以信笔而行，是技法依我，而不是我就技法，其凸显的是文人意趣与情致，往往令观者赏心悦目、神而往之。而与湘中、湘南相对应的湘西南、湘西北少数民族建筑，则多为依山傍水、就地取材的干栏式。它们错落于青山绿水、茂林修竹之间，与之浑然一体、亲切和谐，没有丝毫的矫情和富贵逼人的气息，展示出朴实无华却不乏热烈豁达的民族情怀。

其壁画更富灵动浪漫的精神气象与神秘奇异色彩，呈现的是与湘中、湘南不同的建筑文化和建筑艺术精神，可令观者深刻领悟到人—建筑—自然三者间最为真切友好的关系。

村落生活中的无形文化更是比比皆是，比如：端午吃粽子和中秋吃月饼体现的是民俗文化；清明扫墓体现的是宗族文化；过年时的祭祖祭天体现的是祭祀文化；春天播种，夏天除草，秋天收获，冬天收藏体现的是生产文化。村落中的家法族规与乡规民约更是礼仪文化的集结地，如明代大儒王阳明《南赣乡约》云："故今特为乡约，以协和尔民。自今凡尔等同约之民，皆宜孝尔父母，敬尔兄长，教训尔子孙，和顺尔乡里。死丧相助，患难相恤，善相劝勉，恶相告戒，息讼罢争，讲信修睦。务为良善之民，共成仁厚之俗。

"该乡约中详细规定了人们的行为规范：孝敬父母、尊重长辈、和睦乡邻、戒恶行善、忠厚仁义等。人们正是秉承着这些行为规范代代相传，生生不息，积淀成深厚的文化内涵。真所谓"小村落，大文化"！

中国村落及其文化呈现出鲜明的个性特征，主要表现在四个方面。

一、村落的活态性特征

"活态"是传统村落文化最突出的特征之一。所谓"活态"，是指传统村落文化呈现独特的生命力，延续数百年甚至上千年而依然发挥着固有的功能，至今仍是传统村落中原住民生活的一部分，如村落的古井依然流水潺潺，为村民生活用水提供方便；池塘依旧发挥着生态调节的功能；还有小桥、古树，风景犹在；祠堂、古塔等建筑虽然改变了原始功能，但在居民心中依然是神圣之所，意义未泯；传统的方言依然是村落中交流的主要方式；祖宗的灵位依旧立在神龛上面，被恭敬地供奉着；街道古巷里村落历史的足迹清晰可辨；各种故事、历史传说依然回荡在村落的上空。所以，传统村落被誉为"活化石""活态博物馆"。

费孝通说："祖先们在这地方混熟了，他们的经验也必然就是子孙们所会得到的经验。时间的悠久是从谱系上说的，从每个人可能得到的经验说，却是同一方式的反复重演。同一戏台上演着同一的戏，这个班子里演员所需要记得的，也只有一套戏文。他们个别的经验，就等于世代的经验。经验无需不断累积，只需老是保存。"又说："当一个人碰着生活上的问题时，他必然能在一个比他年长的人那里问得到解决这问题的有效办法，因为大家在同一环境里，走同一道路，他先走，你后走；后走的所踏的是先走的人的脚印，口口相传，不会有遗漏。

"费孝通揭示了传统村落中两个很重要的文化现象：经验与传承。在传统村落中，世世代代累积的经验就是很重要的村落文化。而这种经验的累积，人们并不是用文字的方式记录下来，而是通过口传和不断重复践行的方式传承下来。

简而言之，传统村落文化虽然传承了数百年甚至上千年，但依然发挥着固有的功能。我们从现有的村落原住民的生产生活中，穿越时空的隧道，依然能感受到数百年甚至上千年前他们的祖先生活的情形。

城邑中的精英文化，往往是由文化精英们通过文字记录的方式传播的，并保存在典籍中；传统村落中原住民更多的是用口口相传、代代相承的方式，在言传身教的行为中传递自己的文化。

相对而言，城邑文化趋于静态，而村落文化是动态的；城邑文化是文字的，村落文化是口语的。在传统村落社会，人们既是文化的创造者，又是传承者和践行者；不仅表现为"知"，而且鲜明地突出"行"，"知"规范"行"，"行"实践"知"。知行合一的活态，正是传统村落文化的突出表现。传统村落中这种"活态"的文化，显示出了强大的生命力，成为中华文化中最具象征性的民族文化。因而，研究和保护好这种"活态"的文化，意义十分重大。

这种"活态"文化在历史中数千年了，我们不仅有责任让这种"活态"文化活在当下，而且有义务让其活向未来，成为永远。然而，到了当今世界，在现代工业化和城镇化的进程中，绝大多数传统村落面临着极其严峻的情势。如何保持传统村落文化的"活态"，已经成了当前人类学、社会学、历史学等多学科研究的全新的重要课题，并且这种课题的研究很难以某一单一学科独立地、相对完整地完成。所以，多学科的交叉介入研究，将成为一种必需。

二、村落的血缘性特征

村落的初期形态，最早可以追溯到远古时期的部落生活，并延续数千年而不绝。在其发展历程中，不论是哪种类型的村落形态，也不论村落的形态历经了多少变迁，血缘性一直都是村落文化的重要特征。

在农耕生活的初始时期，人类的生产能力极为低下，仅凭个人几乎很难生存，所以必须依靠群体才能谋生，而最可靠的则是人类与生俱来的血缘关系形成的群体，最有效的是以血缘关系为基础的生活方式。可以想见，人类最早的群体应该是以血缘关系为纽带的氏族。恩格斯指出："一定历史时代和一定地区内的人们生活于其下的社会制度，受着两种生产的制约：一方面受劳动的发展阶段的制约，另一方面受家庭的发展阶段的制约。劳动越不发展，劳动产品的数量、从而社会的财富越受限制，社会制度就越在较大程度上受血族关系的支配。

"在远古时代，生产力极其低下，单靠个人的独立生活是不可想象的，只有依靠血缘亲族团体才能生存下去。这时，人们的血缘关系与地位显得尤为重要和突出，它支配着人们的一切。"全盛时期的氏族制度……其前提是生产极不发达，因而……部落始终是人们的界限，无论对另一部落的人来说，或者对他们自己来说，都是如此：部落、氏族及其制度，都是神圣不可侵犯的，都是自然所赋予的最高权力，个人在感情、思想和行动上始终是无条件服从的。"在远古部落时期，血缘关系是最强有力的联系纽带。

摩尔根在谈到部落联盟建立条件时说："氏族所体现的亲属感情、各氏族的同宗关系，以及他们的方言仍能相互理解，这三者为联盟提供了重要的因素。"在远古时期的部落内，血缘关系可以说是最根本的关系，而没有任何血缘关系的人几乎很难在一个部落内立足。

到了西周时期，血缘关系进一步引申出以家族为主的宗法制。在远古时期的部落社会为了生存而自发形成的以血缘为基础的群体关系，到了"西周，不仅没有采取过破坏氏族的改革，反而经过'维新'，把旧的氏族机关和氏族制度大量移用到阶级社会中，这就不能不给血缘关系的保存留下很大余地"。

"族者，凑也，聚也。谓恩爱相流凑也。上凑高族，下至玄孙，一家有吉，百家聚之，合而为亲，生相亲爱，死相哀痛，有会聚之道，故谓之族。"一个家族长期居住在同一个地方，动辄数代至十数代甚至数十代，于是，在长期的生产生活过程中，就慢慢形成了"聚族而居"的以家族宗法制为中心的村落社会结构。

家族宗法制是中国古代社会独特的社会结构与制度。中国原始社会中以婚姻和血缘关系组合而成的家族制度，在阶级社会中发展为维护剥削阶级世袭特权的家族宗法制。商代奴隶制在血缘关系基础上形成种族奴隶制国家，周代"封诸侯、建同姓"把家族宗法组织作为奴隶制国家的组织形态。此后，封建制虽然取代了奴隶制，但是家族宗法制的社会组织并没有改变。最直接的原因是适应于奴隶制的家族宗法制并没有妨碍于封建制，恰恰相反，家族宗法制又继续适应甚至更加适应封建制。

战国秦汉以来的乡、里、聚、邑、连、闾组织或伍、什编制，以及里正、父老、廷椽、啬夫等基层属吏，仍然代表着社会广泛存在的家族宗法制组织的统治。历代封建王朝不断更迭，家族宗法制却基本上以不变应万变（形式上和部分的"质"有所衍变，但其社会"细胞"的"内核"基本不变）。家族宗法制始终是中国古代直到民主革命前中国社会结构的基本"细胞"。中国封建社会的生产方式、社会组织形式、阶级关系和阶级斗争特点、上层建筑，无不受到家族宗法制的制约和影响。家族宗法制的稳定性、顽固性和不变性，是中国封建社会长期延续的重要原因。

一边保持着家族或氏族组织，一边又以家族共居，组成一个村落的情况，在我国少数民族中更为普遍。

如云南基诺族村寨一般包括数个具有血亲或姻亲关系的父系大家族；傈僳族的村落组成，一般分为三种形式，一是以一个氏族内的一个大家族单独组成，二是由同一氏族内的两个或多个大家族联合组成，三是由几个不同氏族的家族混合组成；在傣族中，有时一个村寨就只属于一个家族，有时一个村寨由几个家族和一些零星户组成；在湘、桂、黔三省边界相连的广大地区，侗族、苗族的村落，不少是以房亲或者房族为构建形态的，一个寨子或好几个寨子都是由同族同姓的房亲、房族组成的。

少数也有外姓杂住其间，但外姓居民的几房在形成上也是由其内在房亲构成的。由此可见，地缘关系和血缘关系是并存的。

"聚族而居"的生活方式凸显了村落中的血缘关系，尤其是在人类社会的早期，血缘关系起着很重要的维系作用。在中国传统社会，小农经济一直是长达数千年的经济格局与形式，血缘关系也一直在传统社会尤其是在传统村落中起着不可替代的作用，并因此形成了以父系血缘为基础的家族宗法制和亲属关系。

费孝通说："我们的格局……好像把一块石头丢在水面上所发生的一圈圈推出去的波纹。每个人都是他社会影响所推出去的圈子的中心。被圈子的波纹所推及的就发生联系。每个人在某一时间某一地点所动用的圈子是不一定相同的。"费孝通在这里很形象、生动、深刻地指出了中国传统社会中以血缘为中心所形成的"这种丢石头形成同心圆波纹的性质"的差序结构，在传统社会中，这种"血缘圈"发挥了重要的作用。

三、村落的地域性特征

中国幅员辽阔，南方和北方纬度差别相当大，气候不同，地质内在构造与地貌特征都不尽相同。因而，传统村落文化呈现出鲜明的地方特色。"十里不同风，百里不同俗"，正是这种地域性特征的鲜活说明。一个村落的文化，往往与其所在的环境息息相关，不同的地域有不同的地形海拔、土质水分、光照温度、日月潮汐、风霜雨雪等影响因素，物种作物的生长发育与土壤、水质、气温、气压、湿度、植被等都有密切的关系。所以，地域不同，不仅影响村落的形成，而且会形成不一样的文化。俗话说，"一方水土养一方人"——一方具有自身独特生活方式的人。

从这个基础出发，我们也可以说，一方水土滋生一方文化。比如，天井是传统村落中常见的建筑。在我国南方建筑中，天井一般南北方向开口狭窄，东西方向狭长，这样可以为建筑提供充足的自然采光，同时强烈的太阳光也不会直接射透天井。而在北方，天井南北方向开口比较大，成为人们晒太阳的理想场所。同样是天井，南北地域的不同直接导致了不同的天井建筑样式与建筑空间，以至形成不同的文化。

民间常有"天赋地造"之说，这在村落建筑材料上反映得尤为突出。不同的地域生产不同的建筑材料，因而人们常常因地制宜地选择当地适当的材料来构建各种建筑。比如，产石地区多石构，不仅柱梁墙是石质材料，就连能遮阳挡雨的"瓦"也是天然的"石片瓦"，而非人工烧制的陶瓦。产木地区多干栏式建筑，产竹地区搭竹楼，黄土高原多窑洞。也有同时使用竹木材料的，南方地区由于多雨潮湿，所以多采用干栏式结构，而北方地区却多采用抬梁式结构。

概而言之，不同地域、不同民族所兴建的传统村落，是不同地域的不同原住民祖先因地制宜，依据当地所特有的自然物产条件与气候光照温度条件，以当地的材料结合当地的建筑工艺和智慧所营造出来的，有着鲜明浓郁的地域特征和民族个性。

不仅仅是建筑不同，饮食习惯也明显不同，通常说"南甜、北咸、东辣、西酸"，虽不尽准确，但大致反映出不同地方的人们饮食习俗的不同。"鲁菜""粤菜""湘菜""川菜""徽菜""淮扬菜""浙菜""闽菜"这"八大菜系"，显示出了更加清晰的地方差异性。

即使像小搬运这样的习俗，各地在挑、担、抬、背、扛、提、搭、推、驮等方式上也有明显的不同。同样是搬运泥沙，有的习惯于肩挑，有的习惯于头顶，有的习惯于背运，有的习惯于手提等，千差万别，各具传统习惯、习俗的特色。

地域性是传统村落文化在空间形态上所显示的特征。地域性特征还突出地反映了传统村落文化的多样性。因而，我们在认识、研究传统村落文化时不能不充分考虑到其地域特征，否则很容易抹杀地域村落的文化形态与个性，也就意味着丢失村落文化的多样性和丰富性。

四、村落的封闭性特征

有人曾经对越南的一个村庄做出这样的描述："浓密的竹林掩映着典型的越南村庄，荆棘篱笆环绕着村舍。村民们居住在绿竹屏蔽之后，就像居住在神话故事中的魔圈里面。周围的田野提供了他们所需要的物产，他们躲在自己造就的保护圈内，不愿与陌生人打交道，甚至不愿意与政府打交道。比如给政府交税吧（这是他们与政府的主要联系），他们就按一个整体由社区统一上交。村庄是这片土地的主宰，是这个国家的支柱，但他们又保持着内部自治和地区范围的自给自足的经济。"这虽然是对越南村落的描述，但是与过去传统社会中的中国传统村落的生活形态有基本的一致性。

由于大多数村落位于乡野僻静之地，加上古代社会道路交通欠发达等要素的制约，村落与外部社会缺少交往，信息较为闭塞。再加上在以小农经济为主体的传统社会，农业生产的自给自足性强，无须与外部社会进行过多的物质交换，从而导致了村落事实上往往成了一个比较独立的、半封闭型的、鸡犬相闻而不相往来的"小国寡民"社会。村落的封闭性主要表现在如下三个方面。

其一，人口流动少。"乡土社会是安土重迁的，生于斯、长于斯、死于斯的社会。不但是人口流动很小，而且人们所取给资源的土地也很少变动。"在传统社会，在一个地方出生的人，往往就在这个地方长大、结婚、生子、变老，一直到死去；人们很少流动，即使外出，老了，也要叶落归根；死了，即使千里万里，也要把棺材运回来，葬在故土里。所以，在没有发生历史变故或自然变故的情况下，一个村落自形成之日起，就在很大程度上一直是几个姓氏，很少发生变动。房子、土地、山林乃至墓地，都是一代一代地传下去的，不会有太大的变动。

其二，土地依赖与生产的封闭性。马克思论述法国农民的时候说："小农人数众多，他们的生活条件相同，但是彼此间并没有发生多种多样的关系。他们的生产方式不是使他们互相交往，而是使他们互相隔离。这种隔离状态由于法国的交通不便和农民的贫困而更为加强了。他们进行生产的地盘，即小块土地，不容许在耕作时进行分工，应用科学，也就没有多种多样的发展，没有各种不同的才能，没有丰富的社会关系。每一个农户差不多都是自给自足的，都是直接生产自己的大部分消费品，因而他们取得生活资料多半是靠与自然交换，而不是靠与社会交往。

一小块土地，一个农民和一个家庭；旁边是另一小块土地，另一个农民和另一个家庭。一批这样的单位就形成一个村子。……广大群众，便是由一些同名数简单相加而形成的，就像一袋马铃薯是由袋中的一个个马铃薯汇集而成的那样。"马克思的"马铃薯之喻"生动反映了小农社会独立、封闭的生产关系。考诸中国传统村落，长期以来，农民的生产无不是独立自封的状态。费孝通说："乡下人离不了泥土，因为在乡下住，种地是最普通的谋生办法。

"向土地求生，是小农社会中乡下人谋生最直接、最简单的方式，他们的生产对象就是土地，"土地是他们的命根子"。由于土地有限，生产力低下，人们要谋生，必须在土地上花费大量的精力，以致他们没有更多的时间和精力从事多样性的生产，也无财力改善生产工具和生产条件。因而，在土地不增加的前提下，只有不断地在土地上付出更多的时间和精力，对土地付出的劳力越多，人们对土地的依附就越紧密，他们只能日复一日、年复一年地在土地上谋生，因而，完全"被土地所囿住"。

向土地求生的生产理念，早已经深入村落原住民的骨髓里，以致现在跟随子女进入城市居住的不少乡民，都试图在城市小区的周边寻找适宜土地，播撒生产的种子，有些甚至把土挑到房顶，自己"制作"小型耕地，达到播种的目的。所以，在乡下人的脑海里，似乎只要有土地，他们的第一个想法就是播种，似乎也只有在土地里播种生产他们才觉得踏实可靠，他们的生产观念完全被局限在土地上了。

其三，生活独立与封闭性。乡下人在土地上播种，依靠土地谋生，生产的目的是自我谋生，所有的产品最终都是为了满足自己的生活，生活所需也基本上由自己生产。"几千年来都是个体经济，一家一户就是一个生产单位。"从生产到消费，是一条完整的封闭的生产生活链，这种建立在以家庭为单位的自给自足基础之上的生产方式，没有分工，相对独立而没有彼此的依赖，本质上是封闭的。再者，在一个相对平和的村落社会中，每个家庭都可以自食其力，平时的生产生活一般不需要他人的帮助，只在偶然的和临时的状态中（如婚丧）才求助于人。生活上，以家庭为单位绝对独立的这种自食其力，客观上不仅形成了人际关系的封闭，而且封闭了人们的思想。

生产的脆弱性，则从根本上限制了小农扩大生活交往的条件，并促使其易于产生保守的心理而排斥外在世界。这是因为交换往往对劳动效率较高的生产者有利，劳动效率高的、不直接从事生活资料生产的人，往往参与交换的积极性高、需求旺盛。而小农由于劳动效率较低，他们参与集市交换往往是不划算的。因此，从根本上说，小农是不愿意拿辛勤劳作获得的生活资料来参与交换的，他们总是最大限度地自我满足家庭需求，只有在迫不得已时才参与少量的交易行为。

另外，在传统村落社会中，村落相对保持孤立状态，村落与村落之间的接触本来就不多，不仅很难有产品交换发生，而且其他相关信息的传播也是相当有限的。正如费孝通所指出的，"乡土社会的生活是富于地方性的。地方性是指他们活动范围有地域上的限制，在区域间接触少，生活隔离，各自保持着孤立的社会圈子"。一般来说，在生于斯、长于斯、死于斯的乡土社会，个人是可以在自己的"一亩三分地"上自食其力生活的，但这也并不意味着乡民就不需要伙伴。

事实上，在重大节庆、婚丧和农忙等偶然性的、临时性的状态之中，仍是需要其他乡民一起协助的。但是，总体上而言，在传统中国，几乎每个村落都拥有一个相对完整的生产生活系统，除了基本的徭役、兵役和诉讼等，村落几乎很少与外部世界特别是朝廷发生直接接触。

English

Section 3: Characteristics of Chinese villages

After people settled down, for survival, they inevitably carried out production, life, and reproduction within a certain scope. In the process of production and life, they continuously accumulated relevant experience, farming to make a living, builDing houses to live in, and communicating to get along.

Over time, with continuous development, corresponding culture emerged. Generally speaking, the category of traDitional village culture refers to the sum of all material and non-material culture formed in the process of series of production and life carried out by people on the basis of communal living in traDitional agricultural society.

That is to say, traDitional village culture includes not only tangible architectural culture, but also the "people" living in traDitional villages, and all tangible and intangible cultural forms created and inherited by "people."

Tangible and explicit cultural forms are mostly reflected in traDitional architecture, and even intangible culture is emboDied and reflected in architecture. Taking Hunan in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River as an example, the mansion-style architecture in central Hunan is often a large courtyard with one family or one clan as a whole.

Its architecture faithfully follows the ritual and music order of traDitional Han culture from spatial layout to functional emboDiment, and even the significance of institutional culture is more important than the actual demand for residential function.

For example, Zeng Guofan's family mansion in Shuangfeng is a model of Confucian residential hierarchy and institutional culture.

"The center is the hall, the left is honorable, the right is secondary," "the east steps are for the host, the west wing is for guests," without the slightest overstepping or negligence, which can be described as "orderly." In contrast, in the villages around Chenzhou in southern Hunan where people live together as clans, there are often independent houses connected to each other, forming a village of grand momentum as a whole.

Although each house also emboDies the traDitional spirit of ritual and music order, from a larger pattern perspective, inDividual houses are relatively independent from each other, yet maintained within the large framework system of a clan, matched with public builDings such as ancestral halls.

Under the basic system of Confucian ethical culture of "carefully attenDing to the funeral rites of parents and following them when gone with due sacrifices" and "the old and young are in order, the honorable and humble are Distinguished," the independent spatial layout facilitates the creation of relatively relaxed interpersonal relationships and survival concepts, and the inDividual's subjective desire for independence can basically be respected in the objective spatial layout, forming an obvious Difference from the large courtyards in central Hunan that completely submerge inDividuals (people) in intangible institutional culture.

This Difference is not only reflected in architectural culture, but also in the murals of builDings, showing two completely Different tones in central and southern Hunan.

The murals on the mansion-style manor builDings in central Hunan mostly show solemn and serious themes with the subject content of human relations and order education, like family instructions, with the persuasive function of education and helping human relations exceeDing the aesthetic pleasure that painting art itself should possess.

Even drama themes that should make people relaxed are covered with a somewhat solemn majesty. In southern Hunan, however, personalized artistic expression is very prominent and typical.

Scenes of family instructions with proper posture are rarely seen, while purely appreciative landscapes, pavilions, flowers, birds, figures, and the pine, bamboo, plum, and orchid themes preferred by scholars become the mainstream.

From the perspective of painting techniques, the mural techniques in central Hunan emphasize regularity and rigor, all showing the atmosphere of orthodox culture, making viewers unconsciously become solemn, serious, and respectful and awed.

The murals in southern Hunan do not have too many technical讲究 and constraints, with the brush following the will and painting arising from interest, so painting freely, with technique following me rather than me following technique, highlighting the literati's interest and sentiment, often making viewers feel delighted and fascinated.

In contrast, the ethnic minority architecture in southwestern and northwestern Hunan corresponding to central and southern Hunan is mostly stilt-style (ganlan) built accorDing to local conDitions and using local materials.

They are scattered among green mountains, clear waters, and dense forests and bamboo groves, integrating with them as one, intimate and harmonious, without the slightest affectation or oppressive wealth, showing a simple and unadorned yet warm and open-minded ethnic sentiment.

Their murals are even more rich in agile and romantic spiritual atmosphere and mysterious and strange colors, presenting a Different architectural culture and architectural artistic spirit from central and southern Hunan, allowing viewers to deeply comprehend the most genuine and friendly relationship among humans—architecture—nature.

Intangible culture in village life is even more ubiquitous.

For example: eating zongzi during the Dragon Boat festival and eating mooncakes during the Mid-Autumn festival reflect folk culture; sweeping tombs during the Qingming festival reflects clan culture; ancestor and heaven worship during the New Year reflects sacrificial culture; sowing in spring, weeDing in summer, harvesting in autumn, and storing in winter reflect production culture.

family rules, clan laws, and village rules and conventions in villages are even more gathering places of ritual culture. For example, the great Confucian scholar Wang Yangming of the Ming dynasty wrote in the Southern jiangxi village Covenant: "Therefore, we now specially make this village covenant to harmonize you people.

From now on, all of you who are part of this covenant should be filial to your parents, respect your elders, teach your children and grandchildren, and harmonize your villages.

Help each other in death and mourning, sympathize with each other in hardship and Disaster, encourage each other in good, warn each other against evil, cease lawsuits and Disputes, emphasize trust and cultivate harmony.

Strive to be good people and together form a culture of benevolence and generosity." This village covenant stipulates in detail people's behavioral norms: being filial to parents, respecting elders, being harmonious with neighbors, abstaining from evil and doing good, being loyal and benevolent, etc.

It is precisely by adhering to these behavioral norms that people pass them down from generation to generation, endlessly, accumulating into profound cultural connotations. Truly, "small villages, great culture"!

Chinese villages and their culture present Distinct inDividual characteristics, mainly manifested in four aspects.

I. The Living Characteristic of villages

"Living" (huotai) is one of the most prominent characteristics of traDitional village culture.

The so-called "living" means that traDitional village culture presents unique vitality, continuing for hundreds or even thousands of years while still performing its inherent functions, and is still part of the lives of inDigenous inhabitants in traDitional villages today.

For example, the ancient wells in villages still flow with water, proviDing convenience for villagers' domestic water; ponds still perform ecological regulation functions; there are also small bridges and ancient trees, the scenery remains; although builDings such as ancestral halls and ancient pagodas have changed their original functions, they are still sacred places in the hearts of residents, with unDiminished significance; traDitional Dialects are still the main means of communication in villages; ancestral spirit tablets are still placed on shrines, reverently enshrined; the footprints of village history are clearly Discernible in ancient streets and alleys; various stories and historical legends still echo above the villages.

Therefore, traDitional villages are praised as "living fossils" and "living museums."

Fei Xiaotong said: "When ancestors have become familiar with this place, their experience will inevitably be the experience that their descendants will obtain. The length of time is spoken of in terms of genealogy; from the perspective of the experience each person may obtain, it is the repeated performance of the same way.

The same play is performed on the same stage, and what the actors in this troupe need to remember is only one set of play text. Their inDividual experience equals the experience of generations.

Experience does not need continuous accumulation, it only needs to be preserved." He also said: "When a person encounters a problem in life, he can inevitably ask someone older than him for an effective solution to this problem, because everyone is in the same environment, walking the same road; he walks first, you walk later; what the later walker steps on are the footprints of the earlier walker, passed down by word of mouth, without omission." Fei Xiaotong revealed two very important cultural phenomena in traDitional villages: experience and inheritance.

In traDitional villages, the experience accumulated over generations is very important village culture. And this accumulation of experience is not recorded by people in writing, but inherited through oral transmission and continuous repeated practice.

In short, although traDitional village culture has been inherited for hundreds or even thousands of years, it still performs its inherent functions. From the production and life of existing village inDigenous inhabitants, through the tunnel of time and space, we can still feel the living conDitions of their ancestors hundreds or even thousands of years ago.

Elite culture in cities is often spread through written records by cultural elites and preserved in classics; inDigenous inhabitants in traDitional villages more often use the method of oral transmission and generational inheritance, passing on their culture through words and deeds.

Relatively speaking, urban culture tends to be static, while village culture is dynamic; urban culture is written, while village culture is oral.

In traDitional village society, people are both the creators of culture and the inheritors and practitioners; not only manifested as "knowing," but also prominently突出 "doing," "knowing" regulates "doing," "doing" practices "knowing." The living state of the unity of knowledge and action is precisely the outstanDing manifestation of traDitional village culture.

This "living" culture in traDitional villages shows strong vitality and becomes the most symbolic ethnic culture in Chinese culture. Therefore, researching and protecting this "living" culture is of great significance. This "living" culture has existed for thousands of years in history.

We not only have the responsibility to let this "living" culture live in the present, but also the obligation to let it live into the future, becoming eternal. However, in today's world, in the process of modern industrialization and urbanization, the vast majority of traDitional villages face an extremely severe situation.

How to maintain the "living" state of traDitional village culture has become a brand-new and important research topic in multiple Disciplines such as current anthropology, sociology, and history, and research on this topic is Difficult to complete independently and relatively completely by a single Discipline.

Therefore, interDisciplinary research will become a necessity.

II. The Blood-Line Characteristic of villages

The initial form of villages can be traced back to tribal life in ancient times and has continued for thousands of years without interruption. In its development process, no matter what type of village form, and no matter how many changes the village form has undergone, blood-line nature has always been an important characteristic of village culture.

In the initial period of agricultural life, human productivity was extremely low, and it was almost Difficult for inDividuals to survive alone, so they had to rely on groups to make a living. The most reliable was the group formed by innate blood relations, and the most effective was the lifestyle based on blood relations.

It is conceivable that the earliest human groups should have been clans bonded by blood relations.

Engels pointed out: "The social system under which people live in a given historical era and a given region is conDitioned by two kinds of production: on the one hand by the stage of development of labor, and on the other by the stage of development of the family.

The less developed labor is, the smaller the quantity of its products, and hence the less the social wealth, the more predominantly the social order is dominated by kinship ties." In ancient times, with extremely low productivity, independent living by inDividuals alone was unimaginable, and only by relying on blood kinship groups could they survive.

At this time, people's blood relations and status were particularly important and prominent, dominating everything about people. "The clan system in its prime... presupposes extremely undeveloped production, and therefore...

the tribe always remained the boundary for people, whether in relation to people of another tribe or in relation to themselves: tribe, clan and their institutions were sacred and inviolable, the supreme power bestowed by nature, to which the inDividual was unconDitionally subject in feeling, thought and action." In ancient tribal periods, blood relations were the strongest bond.

Morgan said when Discussing the conDitions for the establishment of tribal alliances: "The kinship feeling emboDied in the clans, the common ancestry of the various clans, and their Dialects still being mutually intelligible, these three provided important factors for the alliance." Within ancient tribes, blood relations can be said to be the most fundamental relationship, and people without any blood relations could hardly gain a foothold in a tribe.

By the Western Zhou period, blood relations further evolved into the patriarchal clan system centered on families.

The group relations based on blood formed spontaneously for survival in ancient tribal society, by the Western Zhou, "not only was there no reform to destroy the clan, but through 'renewal,' the old clan organs and clan systems were largely transferred into class society, which inevitably left much room for the preservation of blood relations."

"clan (zu) means gathering, assembling. It means love and kindness flow together.

From high ancestors down to great-great-grandchildren, when one family has auspicious events, a hundred families gather, becoming kin through union, loving each other in life, mourning each other in death, with the way of gathering, hence called clan." A family living in the same place for a long time, often for several to more than ten or even dozens of generations, thus, in the long process of production and life, gradually formed a village social structure centered on the family patriarchal system of "living together as a clan."

The family patriarchal system is a unique social structure and system in ancient Chinese society. The family system formed by the combination of marriage and blood relations in primitive Chinese society developed into the family patriarchal system maintaining the hereDitary privileges of the exploiting class in class society.

Shang dynasty slavery formed a racial slavery state on the basis of blood relations, and the Zhou dynasty "enfeoffed princes and established same-surname states" taking family patriarchal organizations as the organizational form of the slavery state.

Thereafter, although feudalism replaced slavery, the social organization of the family patriarchal system Did not change. The most Direct reason is that the family patriarchal system adapted to slavery Did not hinder feudalism; on the contrary, the family patriarchal system continued to adapt to and even better adapt to feudalism.

Since the Warring states, Qin, and Han dynasties, grassroots organizations such as xiang, li, ju, yi, lian, lü or wu, shi systems, as well as grassroots officials such as li zheng (village head), fulao (village elders), tingyuan (suborDinate officials), and sefu (tax collectors), still represented the rule of the widely existing family patriarchal organizations in society.

As feudal dynasties changed continuously, the family patriarchal system basically remained unchanged in response to changes (with changes in form and partial "quality," but the "core" of its social "cell" basically unchanged).

The family patriarchal system was always the basic "cell" of Chinese social structure from ancient times until before the democratic revolution.

The mode of production, forms of social organization, class relations and characteristics of class struggle, and superstructure of Chinese feudal society were all constrained and influenced by the family patriarchal system.

The stability, stubbornness, and unchangeability of the family patriarchal system were important reasons for the long-term continuation of Chinese feudal society.

Maintaining family or clan organizations while living together as families to form a village is more common among ethnic minorities in China.

For example, Jinuo villages in Yunnan generally include several patrilineal extended families with blood or marriage relations; Lisu village composition generally takes three forms: first, formed independently by one extended family within one clan, second, formed by the union of two or more extended families within the same clan, third, formed by the mixture of families from several Different clans; among the Dai, sometimes a village belongs to only one family, sometimes a village consists of several families and some scattered households; in the vast area connecting the borders of Hunan, Guangxi, and Guizhou provinces, many Dong and Miao villages are constructed with qinqin (branch relatives) or fangzu (branch clans) as the form, with one village or several villages all composed of qinqin and fangzu of the same clan and same surname.

Occasionally there are people of other surnames living among them, but the few households of other surnames are also composed of their internal qinqin in formation. Thus, geographical relations and blood relations coexist.

The lifestyle of "living together as a clan" highlights the blood relations in villages, especially in the early stages of human society, blood relations played a very important role in maintaining cohesion.

In traDitional Chinese society, the small-scale peasant economy has been the economic pattern and form for thousands of years, and blood relations have also played an irreplaceable role in traDitional society, especially in traDitional villages, thus forming the family patriarchal system and kinship relations based on patrilineal blood.

Fei Xiaotong said: "Our pattern... is like the ripples spreaDing out in circles caused by throwing a stone into the water. Everyone is the center of the circles pushed out by his social influence. Those reached by the ripples of the circles establish connections.

The circles each person activates at a certain time and place are not necessarily the same." Fei Xiaotong here vividly, lively, and profoundly pointed out the Differential mode of association with the nature of "concentric circle ripples formed by throwing a stone" centered on blood in traDitional Chinese society.

In traDitional society, this "blood circle" played an important role.

III. The Regional Characteristic of villages

China has a vast territory, with considerable Differences in latitude between the south and north, Different climates, and Different internal geological structures and landform features. Therefore, traDitional village culture presents Distinct local characteristics.

"Customs Differ every ten li, traDitions Differ every hundred li" is a vivid illustration of this regional characteristic. The culture of a village is often closely related to its environment.

Different regions have Different terrain elevations, soil quality and moisture, light and temperature, sun and moon tides, wind, frost, rain, and snow, and the growth and development of species and crops are closely related to soil, water quality, temperature, air pressure, humiDity, vegetation, etc.

Therefore, Different regions not only affect the formation of villages, but also form Different cultures. As the saying goes, "one side of water and soil nurtures one side of people" — one side of people with their own unique lifestyles. From this foundation, we can also say that one side of water and soil breeds one side of culture.

For example, the courtyard (tianjing) is a common builDing in traDitional villages. In southern Chinese architecture, the courtyard generally has a narrow north-south opening and a long east-west Direction, which can provide sufficient natural lighting for the builDing while preventing strong sunlight from Directly penetrating the courtyard.

In the north, the courtyard has a relatively large north-south opening, becoming an ideal place for people to sunbathe. The same courtyard, due to Differences between north and south regions, Directly leads to Different courtyard architectural styles and architectural spaces, and even forms Different cultures.

There is a common saying of "endowed by heaven and made by earth," which is particularly prominent in village builDing materials. Different regions produce Different builDing materials, so people often choose local appropriate materials accorDing to local conDitions to construct various builDings.

For example, stone-producing areas mostly use stone structures, not only pillars, beams, and walls are stone materials, but even the "tiles" that can shade from sun and rain are natural "stone slab tiles" rather than artificially fired ceramic tiles.

Wood-producing areas mostly have stilt-style builDings, bamboo-producing areas build bamboo builDings, and the Loess Plateau has many cave dwellings. There are also cases of using both bamboo and wood materials.

In southern regions, due to heavy rainfall and humiDity, stilt-style structures are mostly adopted, while northern regions mostly adopt post-and-lintel structures.

In summary, traDitional villages built in Different regions and by Different ethnic groups are created by inDigenous ancestors of Different regions adapting to local conDitions, based on the unique natural product conDitions and climate, light, and temperature conDitions of the local area, using local materials combined with local architectural techniques and wisdom, with Distinct and rich regional characteristics and ethnic inDividuality.

Not only is architecture Different, but eating habits are also obviously Different. It is commonly said "south sweet, north salty, east spicy, west sour," although not entirely accurate, it roughly reflects the Differences in eating customs of people in Different places.

The "Eight Major Cuisines" — "Lu cuisine," "Yue cuisine," "Xiang cuisine," "Chuan cuisine," "Hui cuisine," "Huaiyang cuisine," "Zhe cuisine," "Min cuisine" — show even clearer regional Differences.

Even customs like small-scale transportation have obvious Differences in methods such as carrying on the shoulder, shouldering, lifting, carrying on the back, heaving, lifting,搭, pushing, and驮.

Similarly for transporting sand and mud, some are used to shoulder carrying, some to head carrying, some to back carrying, some to hand carrying, etc., vastly Different, each with traDitional habits and customs characteristics.

Regionality is the characteristic Displayed by traDitional village culture in spatial form. The regional characteristic also prominently reflects the Diversity of traDitional village culture.

Therefore, when understanDing and researching traDitional village culture, we must fully consider its regional characteristics; otherwise, it is easy to obliterate the cultural form and inDividuality of regional villages, which means losing the Diversity and richness of village culture.

IV. The Closed Characteristic of villages

Someone once described a village in Vietnam like this: "Dense bamboo groves shade typical Vietnamese villages, with thorn hedges surrounDing the houses. villagers live behind the green bamboo screen, just like living inside a magic circle in fairy tales.

The surrounDing fields provide the products they need, they hide within the protective circle they have created, unwilling to deal with strangers, even unwilling to deal with the government. For example, paying taxes to the government (this is their main connection with the government), they pay as a whole uniformly by the community.

The village is the master of this land and the pillar of this country, but they maintain internal autonomy and a self-sufficient economy within the regional scope." Although this is a description of Vietnamese villages, it has basic consistency with the life form of traDitional Chinese villages in past traDitional society.

Because most villages are located in remote rural areas, coupled with constraints such as underdeveloped road transportation in ancient society, villages had little interaction with external society, and information was relatively closed.

In adDition, in traDitional society with the small-scale peasant economy as the main body, agricultural production was highly self-sufficient, without the need for excessive material exchange with external society, thus leaDing to villages often becoming relatively independent, semi-closed "small country with few people" societies where "the sounds of chickens and dogs are heard but people do not visit each other." The closed nature of villages is mainly manifested in the following three aspects.

First, low population mobility. "rural society is attached to the land and averse to moving, a society where people are born, grow, and Die here.

Not only is population mobility very small, but the land from which people obtain resources also rarely changes." In traDitional society, people born in one place often grow up, marry, have children, grow old, and eventually Die there; people rarely move, even if they go out, when old, they must return to their roots; when dead, even if thousands of miles away, they must have the coffin transported back and buried in their native land.

Therefore, without historical or natural Disasters, a village, from the day of its formation, has largely remained with several surnames, rarely changing. Houses, land, forests, and even cemeteries are passed down generation after generation, without much change.

Second, land dependence and the closed nature of production. When Discussing French peasants, Marx said: "The small peasants are numerous, and their conDitions of life are identical, but they do not enter into manifold relations with one another. Their mode of production does not bring them into mutual intercourse, but into mutual isolation.

This isolation is aggravated by the bad means of communication in France and by the poverty of the peasants.

The field of production on which they operate, the small plot of land, does not permit of any Division of labour in its cultivation, any application of science, and therefore no Diversity of development, no variety of talent, no wealth of social relationships.

Each inDividual peasant family is almost self-sufficient, Directly produces most of its consumer goods, and thus obtains its means of subsistence more by exchange with nature than by intercourse with society. A small plot of land, a peasant and his family; alongside them another small plot of land, another peasant and another family.

A mass of such units forms a village.... The great mass is formed by the simple adDition of homologous magnitudes, much as a sack of potatoes is formed by the potatoes in the sack." Marx's "potato metaphor" vividly reflects the independent and closed production relations of small-scale peasant society.

Examining Chinese traDitional villages, for a long time, peasants' production has been in an independent and self-enclosed state.

Fei Xiaotong said: "Country people cannot leave the soil, because living in the countryside, farming is the most common way of making a living." Seeking life from the land is the most Direct and simplest way for country people to make a living in small-scale peasant society, and their object of production is the land, "the land is their lifeline." Due to limited land and low productivity, people must spend a great deal of energy on the land to make a living, so much so that they do not have more time and energy to engage in Diversified production, nor the financial resources to improve production tools and conDitions.

Therefore, without an increase in land, they can only continuously invest more time and energy on the land; the more labor invested in the land, the more closely people are attached to the land, they can only make a living on the land day after day, year after year, thus completely "confined by the land." The production concept of seeking life from the land has long penetrated into the bones of village inDigenous inhabitants, so much so that many villagers who now follow their children to live in cities try to find suitable land around urban residential areas to sow production seeds, and some even carry soil to rooftops to "make" small farmland for sowing purposes.

Therefore, in the minds of country people, it seems that as long as there is land, their first thought is to sow, and it seems only by sowing and producing in the land do they feel secure and reliable, their production concepts completely confined to the land.

Third, independence and closed nature of life. Country people sow on the land, rely on the land to make a living, the purpose of production is self-subsistence, all products ultimately are to satisfy their own lives, and life necessities are basically produced by themselves.

"For thousands of years it has been an inDividual economy, with each family as a production unit." From production to consumption, it is a complete closed production and life chain. This production method based on family-unit self-sufficiency has no Division of labor, is relatively independent without mutual dependence, and is essentially closed.

Furthermore, in a relatively peaceful village society, every family can support itself, and daily production and life generally do not need help from others, only seeking help from others in accidental and temporary situations (such as wedDings and funerals).

In life, this absolute independence of self-support centered on the family objectively not only forms the closure of interpersonal relationships, but also closes people's minds.

The fragility of production fundamentally limits the conDitions for peasants to expand life interactions and promotes their tendency to develop conservative psychology and reject the external world.

This is because exchange often benefits producers with higher labor efficiency; those with high labor efficiency who do not Directly produce means of subsistence often have high enthusiasm and demand for participating in exchange. Peasants, due to low labor efficiency, often find it not worthwhile to participate in market exchange.

Therefore, fundamentally, peasants are unwilling to take the means of subsistence obtained through hard work to participate in exchange; they always maximize self-satisfaction of family needs, and only participate in a small amount of transactions when absolutely necessary.

In adDition, in traDitional village society, villages relatively maintain an isolated state, with本来 little contact between villages, not only is product exchange Difficult to occur, but the transmission of other relevant information is also quite limited. As Fei Xiaotong pointed out, "the life of rural society is rich in local character.

Local character means their scope of activity is limited by region, with little contact between regions, life isolation, each maintaining an isolated social circle." Generally speaking, in rural society where people are born, grow, and Die here, inDividuals can live self-sufficiently on their own "one mu and three fen of land," but this does not mean that villagers do not need partners.

In fact, in accidental and temporary situations such as major festivals, wedDings and funerals, and busy farming seasons, assistance from other villagers is still needed.

But overall, in traDitional China, almost every village has a relatively complete production and life system; except for basic corvée, military service, and litigation, villages rarely have Direct contact with the outside world, especially the imperial court.
