聚落中的居址以单间房为主，多间房开始出现。单间房在形式上有椭圆形、圆形、方形、长方形和不规则形，以半地穴式建筑为主，面积普遍不大，偶有案例如北方地区的赤峰兴隆洼遗址，发现2座面积达140平方米的大房子。多间房，如贾湖遗址第三期，就发现有数座半地穴式内留有门槛的房址，属于2~4间的连间房；新郑唐户遗址裴李岗文化时期的房屋有63座，其中60座为单间房，3间为双间房。这种现象在一定程度上反映出新石器时代前期后期的社会结构在发生变化，可能意味着家庭观念初始期或是早期家庭生活的出现。

综上所述，新石器时代前期属于母系氏族社会，社会关系相对简单，是一种原始共产、共食、共享的生产关系。从房址、墓葬和随葬品来看，未见有明显的社会分化，聚落内部的社会成员平等相处，没有形成严密的聚落组织，社会组织形态相对松散。聚落的农耕性质越来越明显，既体现出聚落的变迁与农业的发展密切相关，也说明农业在人们的经济生活中占据越来越重要的位置，诸如此类，在上文中已有所论及，不再详述。

（三）新石器时代后期聚落遗址的特征

新石器时代后期，伴随以原始农业为主的综合经济的繁荣发展，人类社会开始从母系氏族社会向父系氏族社会转型，私有观念日趋明显，并最终形成私有制。建立在私有制基础上的家庭生活成形并迅速发展。这一切都使聚落在规模和性质上发生结构性变化，体现为如下几个具体特征。

聚落数量大幅增多，规模增大。相比新石器时代前期，同一自然地理单元范围内，后期的聚落数量可能是前期的数倍之多。据资料显示，新石器时代晚期，中原地区仰韶文化时期的聚落数量有900余处，是裴李岗文化时期的5倍之多。长江下游新石器时代末期的良渚文化遗址群，在面积约34平方千米的范围内密集分布着100余处遗址。不仅数量增多，聚落的面积也普遍较前期扩大，面积在5万平方米以上的聚落很多，有些聚落有10万平方米，甚至出现几十万平方米的。

譬如，黄河流域的郑州西山遗址有34万余平方米，郑州大河村遗址有30余万平方米；长江流域的鸡鸣城遗址和鸡叫城遗址址均达到15万平方米。尽管（长）江（黄）河流域的聚落面积普遍扩大，但两者相比，黄河流域地区的聚落面积整体上比长江流域地区的大。原因除与人口密度有关以外，更是与文明进程有关，但自然地理条件因素亦不能排除。黄河流域的地势相对较为辽阔，而长江流域尤其是长江以南则多丘陵山谷，不利于大面积的自然农耕与大面积聚落的兴建。当然，这仅仅只是一种基于历史地理与自然及经济地理的判断。

聚落分化为中心聚落与普通聚落，地缘一体化倾向明显。有学者根据聚落面积的大小，把聚落划分为4个等级：特级聚落50万平方米以上，一级聚落30万~49万平方米，二级聚落10万~29万平方米，三级聚落9万平方米及以下。他们还根据这一标准对河南地区仰韶文化时期的聚落进行了划分。以豫西洛阳地区为例，有特级聚落3个，一级聚落7个，二级聚落25个，三级聚落132个。

尽管这种划分带有强烈的人为主观性，不是十分科学，并且聚落面积的大小与聚落的等级地位也未必绝对相当，但是于宏观层面来说，还是可以在一定程度上反映聚落分化为中心聚落与普通聚落这一事实的。从聚落结构和出土遗存等来看，诸如长江流域的城头山遗址、鸡叫城遗址、石家河土城遗址和良渚文化遗址群中的莫角山遗址，黄河流域的临潼姜寨遗址、郑州西山遗址、大河村遗址、尉迟寺聚落遗址和丁公遗址等聚落，不仅在等级和地位上都要高于周边范围内的聚落，而且以其为中心形成聚落群团，中心聚落性质十分明显。

良渚文化遗址群以莫角山为中心，周边分布着100余处遗址。这些都表明，新石器时代后期，在一定的自然地理单元范围内，地缘一体化趋势日趋强烈。这种现象的产生，除血缘因素以外，可能更多的是出于政治、军事防御上对地缘的需求，与聚落生产能力及内需经济也有一定的关系。

聚落的功能区划清晰，体现出一定的规划性。一般而言，在平面布局上，聚落由居住区、手工作坊区（陶窑场）、公共广场、墓葬区和环壕等组成，不仅规划性很强，而且表现出强烈的内聚性特征。譬如，陕西临潼姜寨遗址、西安半坡遗址、宝鸡北首岭遗址、秦安大地湾遗址、安徽大汶口文化的尉迟寺聚落遗址等黄河流域地区的聚落就极为典型。

相比黄河流域，考古发掘所见长江流域聚落的功能区划相对含糊，但事实上，从澧阳平原的城头山遗址、鸡叫城遗址，以及河姆渡遗址和石家河土城等聚落所遗留的城垣、环壕和居住遗址来看，其规划性同样明显，并且很强。例如，城头山遗址虽然城内的功能区划并非十分明确，但从其护城河、夯土城墙和东、西、南、北四门组成的遗迹来看，其显然是经过严密规划与设计的。

环壕型聚落呈现出向城郭发展的趋势。伴随着中心聚落与普通聚落的分化，聚落的发展开始形成明显的两种趋势，其中前者朝城郭方向发展，后者的发展则几近于停滞，属于典型的散布型村落。前者在外观形态上一般有环壕，体现出强烈的军事防御性特征；就聚落建筑而言，除民宅以外，通常还有祭祀遗址和大型公共建筑或宫殿式建筑，表现出突出的宗教性、政治性功能。

譬如河南新密古城寨遗址，城内东北部就有两座大型房址，一座为宫殿式建筑，面积近384平方米，另一座为附属建筑，属于廊庑式建筑；石家河文化遗址群中的土城则拥有大型的礼制性建筑，这些都表明，环壕型建筑逐渐发展为城郭。尽管追溯历史，早在距今8 000年前的澧阳平原八十垱遗址就发现了环壕遗迹，距今6 000年前的城头山更是拥有了完整的城垣，但从年代上来说，这类环壕型聚落的大量出现应该是在龙山文化以后。

仅河南龙山文化时期的城郭型聚落，就出现了登封王城岗、辉县孟庄、淮阳平粮台、新密新砦城址、安阳后岗等几十余处。

聚落居址连间房增多，分化明显，地面建筑普遍出现。相比新石器时代前期，这一时期虽然单间房仍十分常见，但连间房明显增多，而且多呈方形和长方形。譬如安徽蒙城尉迟寺遗址的居住建筑，多以两间或两间以上的房址为一组，分布于壕沟内侧，从北向南有12排，零星房址2间。郑州大河村仰韶文化三期的聚落房址，除1座为半地穴式房址以外，其余房址均为地面建筑，而且房址多数为两间或两间以上，其中有并列四连间1座，并列二连间2座。

不仅如此，这期间的居住空间明显经过了一定的室内装饰，有些用草拌泥垒筑，有些则采用木骨泥墙，房间地面也经过处理，有的经过烧烤，有的用料礓石铺就或草拌泥铺抹。河南邓州八里岗仰韶文化晚期、大河村文化三期的聚落居室，都有类似的处理。这些不仅表明史前建筑技术取得了较大进步，而且反映出史前社会发生了分化，形成了不同阶层群体。

上述聚落变迁的特征显示，新石器时代后期人类的社会关系发生了转变，已不再是简单的原始共产、共食、共享的生产关系。不论是聚落与聚落之间，还是聚落内部的成员之间，都呈现出明显的分化现象，社会组织形态严密，有了贫富、等级和地位的区别。正是这一系列转型，促使着人类社会向阶级社会进化，并开始向文明社会迈进。

（四）史前聚落遗址的价值意义

从史前聚落的发展及其变迁来看，我们大致可以得出如下几点历史认知。

首先，村落的起源与农业的兴起密切相关，尽管农业的出现并不是村落产生的唯一条件，但人类从"居无定所"的迁徙流动生活方式逐步走向定居生活，由早期的穴居、巢居发展到固定居民点，再到村落的产生和村落群的形成，及至城邑和国家的出现，都无不打上了浓厚的农耕烙印。从村落的产生到国家的形成，不仅意味着中华大地从分散走向统一，而且是早期人类社会从血缘、地缘进化到文明的兴起和整合。在农业发达地区的长江流域、黄河流域，乃至北方地区，其早期村落的发展显示，中华文化的起源是多源头的。

作为农业发展的先决条件，自然地理条件影响甚至决定着早期村落及其文化的生成与发展。村落在起源阶段，尽管因人类本身及所处地域环境的不同而具有族群性、地域性和多样性的特点，但由于早期人类在生存驱动上的相同性，村落也呈现出一定的统一性。可以肯定的是，我国早期村落具有集统一性与多样性于一体的性质。这一性质还显示，村落的变迁除了受土地与人口等因素的制约和刺激外，也与族群、信仰、道德、语言、风俗和地理等因素的变化密切相关。

其次，村落作为我国人类社会进入农耕文明的重要标志，是农林渔牧业人群长期生产、生活、聚居、繁衍和进行政治、经济、文化活动的场所，是相对稳定、明晰的社会单元。它在承载中华民族的历史文化方面具有本源性和传承性的特点。特别是村落和村落中所产生并形成的包括建筑、工具、技术、组织、制度、道德和信仰等在内的物质与非物质文化形态，虽是农耕文明的产物，但被最初的城市最大限度地继承和发展，所以也成了城市及其文化的源头。

尽管国家出现后，部分城市是因各种原因而建造或发展起来的，但不可否认的是，城市文化的源头是村落起源阶段所积淀的文化传统。尽管伴随着早期社会中越来越明显的城乡分野趋势，逐渐形成了城乡两种文化类型和两种经济形态，社会的贫富和地位的分化日渐裂变，但在自古以农立国的中国古代社会，特别是在生产力相对低下的早期农业社会，村落远远不只是一个社会单元和生活单元，更具有哺乳城市、服务国家的意义，在推进城郭发展、维系国家稳定和繁荣方面起到了极为积极的重大作用。

最后，村落作为建立在血缘和地缘基础上的聚落，有自身的范围与活动空间，具有聚族群体性和血缘延续性的文化特质，呈现为封闭性、保守性和地域性等特点，是有形的地域性物质实体空间与血缘性、地缘性乃至亲缘性非物质社会空间的高度重合。因此，讨论村落的起源及其演化的问题，不能仅仅局限于村落的物质实体空间，更要顾及村落的非物质社会空间，尤其要挖掘村落所承载的中华民族形成与发展过程中所发生的历史文化信息及其所映射出的"家国一体"的社会与文化内涵。

村落的起源与早期发展表明：早期人类社会不仅经历了从原始群体到氏族社会，再到部落、部落联盟，进而到民族和国家社会形成的过程，中华民族最初的文化传统也是形成并发展于村落的。它是中国民族文化的逻辑起点与实际历史的起点，隐含着丰富的政治、经济以及包含宗教在内的深层次历史文化信息与内涵。

当然，村落作为一个实际存在的生产生活的聚落空间和相对稳定的社会单元，在进入国家形式后，它的生存与发展理所当然地受到了来自国家的严密管控，但也正因如此，村落与国家、民族的发展更紧密地联系在一起，成了见证国家和民族发展的活证与实证。关于这些，我们将在后续研究中做进一步阐释。

English

Section 2: prehistoric settlement sites

We generally refer to human history before the appearance of writing as prehistory, that is, from the Discovery of early humans until the Shang dynasty period when oracle bone inscriptions were Discovered.

From the perspective of civilization history, the common view is that prehistoric society, i.e., the remote antiquity of Chinese history, was the social stage before the birth of civilized society.

This stage corresponds to what archaeologists call the Stone Age, roughly belonging to the period of human history before the emergence of the Xia dynasty in the 21st century BCE. Archaeologically, "prehistoric society" can be Divided into two stages: the Paleolithic Age and the Neolithic Age.

The former is marked by chipped stone tools, spanning from the origin of humanity to about 10,000 years ago, a period of several million years; the latter is marked by polished stone tools, beginning 10,000 years ago and enDing around 5,000 years ago.

From the perspective of social forms, prehistoric society, as the initial period of the formation and development of human society, roughly experienced several social stages incluDing primitive hordes, clan communes, and tribal alliances. settlements, as places for early human production and life, fully reflect this.

To better reveal and understand the settlement forms of prehistoric society, it is necessary to sort out and interpret the prehistoric settlements Discovered archaeologically in China.

I. Major prehistoric settlement sites in the Yellow River Basin

The Yellow River Basin refers to the nine provinces and regions through which the Yellow River flows: Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, Ningxia, Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi, Shanxi, Henan, and Shandong.

Archaeologically, the Yellow River Basin focuses more on the middle and lower reaches, mainly incluDing five provinces and regions: Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi, Shanxi, Henan, and Shandong.

From archaeological Discoveries, the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River are also the areas where prehistoric settlement sites are most concentrated, most typical, and richest in cultural remains.

Chronologically, the settlement sites in the Yellow River Basin are mainly from the middle and late Neolithic Age; what was Discovered from the Paleolithic Age were mainly residential sites with strong migratory characteristics, not yet possessing the complete elements of villages.

(1) Paleolithic Residential Sites

Archaeological Discoveries of the Paleolithic Age in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River began in the early 1920s.

At that time, French Jesuit and geobiologist Pierre Teilhard de CharDin and Emile Licent conducted geological surveys in the Ordos region of China, and accidentally Discovered early human fossils, chipped stone tools, and mammal fossils at the Salawusu River at the border of Shaanxi and Inner Mongolia, and at Shuidonggou in Ningxia.

The human fossils Discovered here were later named "Ordos Man." This may be the earliest human fossil Discovered in China with a reliable location and stratigraphic position. It was this Discovery that pioneered prehistoric archaeology in the Yellow River Basin of China.

Since then, Paleolithic residential sites and chipped stone tool remains have been continuously Discovered in the middle reaches of the Yellow River, mainly in Shaanxi. To date, human fossils and activity remains from the early, middle, and late Paleolithic Age have all been Discovered in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River.

The more typical and representative clustering phenomena among these relics and remains mainly include the Shuidonggou Basin in Ningxia, the Luonan Basin in Shaanxi, the Fen River Basin in Shanxi, and the Yi-Shu River Basin in Shandong.

1. Shuidonggou Basin, Ningxia

The Shuidonggou Basin is located in Linhe Town, Lingwu city, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, bordering Yinchuan to the west, near Lingwu city to the south, and adjacent to Ordos city, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region to the north.

Since the French paleontologists Teilhard de CharDin and Emile Licent Discovered the Shuidonggou Site in 1923, more than 30 Paleolithic sites have been Discovered in Shuidonggou and its vicinity.

Among them, 14 new sites were Discovered at Shuidonggou, Shijiayao, and Zhangjiayao, and 5 sites were Discovered at Lingercun and Liuhe in Pengyang County, Guyuan city, southern Ningxia. The Shuidonggou Site Discovered in 1923 is one of the earliest Discovered and excavated Paleolithic cultural remains in China.

Since its Discovery, it has undergone multiple excavations, yielDing a large number of chipped stone tools and animal fossils.

Among the tens of thousands of Paleolithic stone tools unearthed from the site, many exhibit strong characteristics of the European Middle-to-Late Paleolithic transition, and some stone artifacts show characteristics of the northern Chinese flake tool industry.

Therefore, it has received extensive attention from the academic community at home and abroad.

This phenomenon of Shuidonggou culture not only reflects possible cultural exchanges and interactions between early human groups in China and European groups, but also inDicates to some extent an inherent relationship between the formation of human culture and great migrations.

Within the surrounDing area of the Shuidonggou Site, 11 residential clusters have been Discovered so far, most within a few hundred meters of each other, with the farthest no more than 1-2 kilometers apart.

The Shijiayao site group and Zhangjiayao site group Discovered in 2002 also show that the various sites of human activity are very close to each other.

2. Luonan Basin, Shaanxi

Shaanxi Province has many Discovered Paleolithic site groups, mainly Distributed in the Luo River and Wei River basins in the eastern and central Guanzhong region, and in the upper Han River and southern Luo River basins in southern Shaanxi, with scattered Distribution in western Guanzhong and northern Shaanxi.

Among them, Guanzhong and southern Shaanxi are dominated by early and middle Paleolithic remains, while northern Shaanxi is more common in late remains. The Luonan Basin in Shaanxi is the most prominent.

The Luonan Basin is located in southeastern Shaanxi Province, between the Taihua Mountains at the eastern foot of the Qinling Mountains and the Mangling Mountains, about 150 kilometers northwest of Xi'an.

The basin is about 70 kilometers long from east to west and 20-30 kilometers wide from north to south, with the Luo River running through it, belonging to the upper reaches of the Luo River.

AccorDing to surveys by relevant archaeologists in the Luonan Basin, 268 Paleolithic sites have been Discovered so far, with more than 13,000 various Paleolithic artifacts collected.

Among these stone artifacts, tool assemblages with Acheulean cultural characteristics popular in Africa and Eurasia, such as hand axes and cleavers, have appeared, incluDing 45 hand axes and 119 cleavers, which can be regarded as the most concentrated Discovery of Acheulean-type artifacts in China to date.

These tools, basically symmetrical on both left-right and front-back sides, are considered the first standarDized tools in human history, fully reflecting the accumulation of technical experience by early humans.

In adDition to the Discovery of such tool assemblages in the Luonan Basin, they have also been found at Liangshan in Hanzhong, Shaanxi in northwest China, the Baise Basin in Guangxi and the inundated area of the Mangtangxi Hydropower Station in Zhijiang, Hunan in regions south of the Yangtze River, and Huzhuashan in Hejin city.

The large north-south span inDicates to some extent that the formation of early human world culture may have involved great exchanges and spread.

In adDition, one cave site named "Huashilang Longyadong" was Discovered in the Luonan Basin, located on the Huashilang hill behind Donghe village in the Luonan Basin, consisting of two closely spaced caves, dating back about 500,000 years.

3. Fen River Basin, Shanxi

The Fen River Basin in Shanxi is also an important area for Paleolithic site Distribution. The main sites include the Dingcun Site in Xiangfen, the Xujiayao Site in Yanggao, and the Xiaochangliang Site in Yangyuan.

The Dingcun Site, Discovered in 1953, is located on the east bank of the Fen River near Dingcun village, Xiangfen County, southern Shanxi. Excavations began in 1954, and three excavation areas were established along the Fen River, uncovering a large number of stone tools and animal fossils.

The stone tools from Dingcun are mainly made of flint, with types incluDing choppers, scrapers, points, and stone balls. The Xujiayao Site, Discovered in 1974, is located at the junction of Yanggao County, Shanxi and Yangyuan County, Hebei.

It has yielded human fossils incluDing parietal bones, occipital bones, and teeth, belonging to about 10 inDividuals, as well as more than 10,000 stone artifacts and a large number of animal fossils. The Xiaochangliang Site in Yangyuan is one of the earliest Paleolithic sites in northern China, dating back about 1.36 million years.

4. Yi-Shu River Basin, Shandong

The Yi-Shu River Basin in Shandong has also Discovered many Paleolithic sites, mainly Distributed in the upper reaches of the Yi River and Shu River. Representative sites include the Xishigou Site in Yiyuan and the Changma Site in Junan.

The Yiyuan Man fossils Discovered in Yiyuan County include skull fragments, teeth, and limb bones, dating back about 400,000-500,000 years, belonging to the stage of Homo erectus.

In summary, the Paleolithic residential sites in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River show two notable characteristics: on one hand, each site represents an independent activity group; on the other hand, sites within a certain range show obvious clustering properties.

There are two possibilities for this phenomenon: first, relic points formed by the migratory activities of the same ethnic group in Different spatio-temporal ranges; second, relic points formed by the activities of Different groups of the same ethnic group or Different ethnic groups in roughly the same spatio-temporal range.

Regardless of the possibility, they at least demonstrate that proximity to water sources was an important principle for early humans in choosing group activity locations. The former is related to the animal instinct of humans to gather, while the latter is the result of human survival experience.

Archaeologist Pei Anping summarized the relationship between Paleolithic site communities and the environment into three models: the riverine model, the basin and river confluence model, and the plain model.

The riverine model is based on the narrow terrace surfaces of rivers, with site groups Distributed in a beaded belt pattern; the basin and river confluence model tends to be larger in scale, with sites relatively compactly clustered; the plain model is based on open piedmont plains, witnessing the trend of site communities moving toward plains.

Essentially, the formation and changes of the Distribution and morphological characteristics of site points are manifestations of early human evolution and the origin of human culture.

(2) Neolithic settlement sites

As mentioned earlier, after entering the Neolithic Age, agriculture began to rise and develop, and the residential sites formed since the Paleolithic Age began to develop toward settlement, scale, and density.

As an important region for the origin of prehistoric agriculture, the Yellow River Basin, compared with other regions, had relatively developed agriculture due to superior natural geographical conDitions.

For this reason, settlements based on agricultural settled life developed to a greater extent in the Yellow River Basin, densely Distributed in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River and northern areas.

In this Discussion, on one hand, we note the importance of geographical zoning of the settlements to be Discussed from a geographical perspective; on the other hand, we should emphasize vertical Division from a chronological perspective to reflect changes in settlements and settlement forms in the early and late Neolithic Age.

1. Early Neolithic settlement sites

Archaeological Discoveries show that the early Neolithic settlement sites in the Yellow River Basin are typified by the Peiligang culture type, Cishan culture type, and Houli culture type.

These cultural types inDicate that after the origin of agriculture, after a relatively long period of development, it gradually became the main sector of the social economy in the middle Neolithic Age.

However, since the early Neolithic Age was still in the early stage of agricultural development, both population and productivity were limited, so the number of settlement sites was not large and the settlement scale was relatively small.

Nevertheless, as important places for early human production and life, settlements can reflect the development status and general social structure of human society in the Yellow River Basin during the early Neolithic Age.

(1) Peiligang Culture settlements

Named after its Discovery at Peiligang village in Xinzheng city, Henan Province, the Peiligang culture is one of the earliest Neolithic cultures Discovered in the Central Plains region and an important source of Chinese civilization.

AccorDing to statistics from the Institute of Archaeology, Chinese academy of Social Sciences, more than 100 Peiligang culture sites have been Discovered so far, Distributed in over 40 counties and cities within Henan Province.

Among them, the central Henan region on the south bank of the Yellow River is more concentrated, with some Distribution in the hilly areas of western Henan and southern Henan. Generally, Peiligang culture sites are not large in area, with small ones being several thousand square meters and large ones being tens of thousands of square meters.

Important settlement sites include the Peiligang Site, the jiahu Site in Wuyang, the Tanghu Site in Xinzheng, and the Egou Beigang Site in Mixian.

The Peiligang Site is the first formally excavated Peiligang culture site, covering an area of about 20,000 square meters, dating back 8,000 years, and is an important early Neolithic cultural remain. Its Discovery filled the historical gap before the Yangshao culture in China.

From 1977 to 1979, archaeologists conducted four excavations of the Peiligang Site, uncovering 114 tombs, one pottery kiln, more than 10 ash pits, and several remains of cave dwellings.

The tombs are basically north-south oriented or southward slightly westward, densely Distributed, and most are rectangular vertical pit earth tombs with no burial implements found.

The jiahu Site in Wuyang, located east of jiahu village, Beiwudu township, Wuyang County, Henan Province, covers an area of 55,000 square meters, dating back 9,000-7,500 years. The site was first excavated in 1961 and has undergone seven excavations in 1983, 1984-1987, 2001, etc., with an excavation area of more than 2,600 square meters.

The site is nearly circular, Divided into east, central, and west zones. Two sections of moats from the middle and late Neolithic Age were Discovered in the southwest and south. The cleared remains include nearly 50 house foundations, 9 pottery kilns, nearly 400 ash pits, and nearly 400 tombs.

The remains and relics in the west zone are more typical, basically reflecting the settlement appearance, with 12 early Neolithic house sites, 2 kiln sites, 42 tombs; 8 middle house sites, 1 kiln site, 154 tombs; 16 late house sites, 1 kiln site, 122 tombs.

The house sites are regularly arranged in groups, all circular or oval semi-subterranean, with single-room and multi-room types, but mainly single-room semi-subterranean, with only a few multi-room ones, whose form is to leave a small threshold inside the house site and successively expand into 2-4 rooms.

The house area is generally not large, mostly within 10 square meters, a few between 10-20 square meters, and the largest one is only 52 square meters. Early, middle, and late remains include inscribed tortoise shells, bone flutes, and rice cultivation remains.

From the overall layout, the early residential area and burial area were not separated, mixed together; in the middle and late periods, separation began, and the trend of orderly grouping of houses was obvious.

The Tanghu Site in Xinzheng, located in the west and south of Tanghu village, Guanyinsi Town, Xinzheng city, Henan Province, is on a corner terrace near the river.

The site covers an area of more than 1.4 million square meters and is a settlement group site spanning Peiligang culture, Yangshao culture, Longshan culture, Erlitou culture, and the Shang, Zhou, Han, Song, Yuan, and Qing periods.

Among them, the remains from the Peiligang culture period include 63 house sites, 207 ash pits, 4 Ditches (1 drainage system), and 1 moat. The house sites are laid out in 4 groups, of which 2 have the characteristic of row layout.

The house site planes include circular, oval, rounded rectangular, and irregular shapes, which can be Divided into single-room and double-room types, mainly single-room with 60 in total, and 3 double-room ones formed by secondary expansion.

There are 6 traces of stove use, located on one side of the room doorway or outside the house site, inDicating that life at that time still had the characteristic of communal eating.

The interior living surfaces and walls were processed, with circular or oval post holes Distributed around the house sites, and some house sites symmetrically Distributed one ash pit on both sides.

From the overall layout of the settlement site, the core residential area is Distributed in the southeast of the settlement site, reflecting a certain awareness of functional zoning, and the combination of house sites and ash pits reflects a centripetal layout.

The Egou Beigang Site in Mixian is a small settlement of the Peiligang culture, covering an area of 8,000 square meters, with an excavation area of 2,747 square meters. A total of 6 circular and square semi-subterranean house sites, 4 ash pits, and 68 tombs were cleared.

The houses are concentrated in the middle of the settlement site, with house areas generally within 10 square meters, and the largest no more than 11 square meters. The east is basically open space, with a few storage pits. The west and northwest are cemeteries, with tombs arranged in order, Divided into several groups.

Except for 8 tombs without grave goods, the rest have varying numbers of grave goods, mainly stone tools such as shovels, axes, sickles, grinDing slabs, and grinDing stones, and pottery vessels, generally 2-8 pieces. This settlement, whether in layout or house area, is small in scale and should belong to a small clan commune residential unit.

From the house structure and grave goods in the tombs, no obvious social Differentiation is yet seen.

(2) Cishan Culture settlements

Named after the Cishan Site in Wu'an, Hebei Province, the Cishan culture belongs to the Neolithic culture of North China, mainly Distributed on the eastern foot of the Taihang Mountains in central and southern Hebei, south to the Zhang River, north to the Juma River and Daqing River basins north of baoDing, and generally concentrated in the Ming River basin in southern Hebei.

Since the Cishan culture is chronologically earlier than the Yangshao culture, archaeologists often refer to it together with the DaDiwan, Lijiacun, and Peiligang cultures as the "pre-Yangshao" culture. Important settlement sites of the Cishan culture include the Cishan Site in Wu'an and the BeifuDi Site in Yi County.

The Cishan Site in Wu'an, located 20 kilometers southwest of Wu'an, Hebei, on the terrace on the north bank of the Ming River southeast of Cishan village, is at the foot of Gu Mountain of the Taihang Mountains, backed by the Cishan Iron Mine to the north and facing the Ming River to the south.

The site has Discovered 2 house sites, 474 ash pits, and nearly 2,000 relics incluDing pottery, stone tools, and bone and horn artifacts. The south and southwest of the Cishan Site are 2 semi-subterranean house sites, oval and circular respectively, with ramps or steps. The house walls may be made of burnt earth with reed impressions.

The house area is generally around 10 square meters. The ash pits are generally storage pits for grain, of which 62 out of 474 ash pits have found grain accumulations such as millet ash, with accumulation thickness of 0.3-2 meters. The ash pits are mainly rectangular, with other forms incluDing circular, oval, and irregular.

Domestic animal bones such as dogs, pigs, sheep, and chickens have also been found in the site, as well as agricultural production tools such as stone axes, stone shovels, stone knives, and stone sickles, and grain processing tools such as stone grinDing slabs and stone grinDing sticks, which fully prove that the Cishan people had relatively developed agriculture.

The rich agricultural remains also inDicate that the Cishan settlement site is a typical agricultural settlement.

The BeifuDi Site in Yi County, located on the terrace of BeifuDi village, 12.5 kilometers southwest of Yi County, Hebei Province, is at the junction of the Taihang Mountains, Hengshan Mountains, and Yanshan Mountains and the border zone with the Hebei Plain.

The surrounDing landform belongs to a broad river valley between low mountains and hills, with the Yi River crossing from west to east in the middle. Since its Discovery in 1985, the site has undergone three formal excavations in 1997, 2003, and 2004, with a proven area of 30,000 square meters.

Different stages of Neolithic cultural remains have been Discovered, with scattered remains from the Shang-Zhou, Han, and Liao-Jin periods locally. Twelve semi-subterranean Neolithic house sites were unearthed, densely Distributed, regularly arranged in plane layout, with three plane shapes: rectangular, nearly square, and nearly circular.

The interior floors have red-burnt earth stove surfaces, with relics incluDing stones, stone materials, and various types of stone artifacts and pottery, with post holes around.

One sacrificial site, nearly rectangular in plane, with a total area of more than 90 square meters, consists of more than 90 relics incluDing small straight-bellied basins, various polished stone tools, jade artifacts, small stone carvings, and crystals.

Among the polished stone tools, a large stone plow 46 centimeters long and fully polished was also found. The sacrificial site may have been a religious place for BeifuDi people to conduct agricultural sacrificial activities, belonging to the public space of religious belief in the village.

(3) Houli Culture settlements

The Houli culture is named after the Houliguanzhuang Site in Linzi District, Zibo city, Shandong Province.

AccorDing to archaeological Discovery data, this culture is mainly Distributed in the piedmont plain zone on the northern side of the Taiyi Mountain system, with its range roughly being the narrow zone from the Zi River in the east to Changqing in the west.

More than 10 sites containing Houli culture remains have been excavated so far, incluDing Xiaojingshan and Xihe in Zhangqiu, Sunjia in Zouping, and southwest of Wande, Zhangguanzhuang, Motianling, and Lüzhuyuan in Changqing. Among them, important sites include the Houli Site, Xiaojingshan Site, and Xihe Site in Zhangqiu.

2. Late Neolithic settlement sites

After the relatively long development of the early Neolithic Age, around 5000 BCE, prehistoric humans entered the late period of primitive society, i.e., the late Neolithic Age, which ended around 3000 BCE.

During this period, agriculture developed to a certain extent, rising to become the main sector of the social economy and occupying a dominant position. The development of agriculture brought abundant food, which in turn promoted rapid population growth.

The Direct impact of population increase on settlements was reflected in two aspects: first, the expansion of settlement scale, because only the expansion of settlement scale could accommodate more population; second, the large increase in the number of settlements, for various reasons, but fundamentally because the means of subsistence produced by limited arable land resources could not meet the needs of the rapidly growing population, so opening up new land and builDing new settlements elsewhere was the best choice.

It was also in this development process that private ownership began to germinate, society began to Differentiate, matrilineal clans transformed into patrilineal clan society, and settlements also began to Differentiate into two types: giant settlements and orDinary settlements, with obvious settlement groups formed around giant settlements, and geopolitical integration became increasingly obvious.

This is most typical in the upper, middle, and lower reaches of the Yellow River, mainly incluDing the Yangshao culture in the middle reaches, the Beixin culture and Dawenkou culture in the lower reaches, the Longshan culture spanning the middle and lower reaches, and the Majiayao culture in the upper reaches, to name but a few.

(1) Majiayao culture settlements

Named after its first Discovery at Majiayao village in Lintao County, Gansu Province, the Majiayao culture belongs to a cultural type of the Yangshao culture developing toward the upper reaches of the Yellow River, dating back about 5,700 years. It includes remains of two types: Banshan and Machang.

The former was Discovered at Banshan in Guanghe County, Gansu Province, and the latter at Machang in Minhe County, Qinghai Province. Majiayao culture settlements are mainly Distributed on both banks and surrounDing areas of the Yellow River and its tributaries such as the Tao River, Huangshui River, and Wei River within Gansu and Qinghai.

AccorDing to incomplete statistics, more than 800 Majiayao culture sites have been Discovered in the Gansu-Ningxia-Qinghai region, incluDing 200 Banshan type sites and more than 600 Machang type sites. Important ones include the Qinggangcha Site in Lanzhou, Gansu and the Caiyuancun Site in Haiyuan, Ningxia.

The Qinggangcha Site in Lanzhou, Gansu is located at Gangjiashan, Qinggang village, south of Lanzhou city, Gansu Province, on a terrace on the south bank of the Yellow River, covering an area of about 80,000 square meters.

Among them, one Banshan-type house site, two storage pits, one kiln site, and one tomb were Discovered, as well as one Machang-type kiln site and one Qijia culture house site.

The second excavation also Discovered three Banpo-type house sites, one storage pit, and three tombs, unearthing a batch of production and living utensils such as stone tools, bone tools, and pottery. These Discoveries inDicate that the Qinggangcha Site had a large time span and was a settlement site with relatively frequent human activities.

The Caiyuancun Site in Haiyuan, Ningxia is located on the slope south of Caiyuancun village, Haiyuan County, Ningxia, at the northern foot of the South Huashan Mountain.

Three sites (Linziliang, Mayingziliang, and Shigou) and five cemeteries (Qiedaoba, Waguanzui, Zhaiziliang, Erlingziwan, and Linziliang) were Discovered, with a total exposed area of 4,780 square meters.

Fifteen house sites, 65 storage pits, one kiln site, one ash Ditch, and 138 tombs were found, unearthing more than 5,000 production and living utensils such as stone tools, bone tools, and pottery.

(2) Yangshao culture settlements

The Yangshao culture is a very important Neolithic culture in the middle reaches of the Yellow River, with a long duration of about 2,000 years, spanning from 5000 BCE to 3000 BCE. The Yangshao culture is named after the Yangshao village Site first Discovered in Mianchi County, Henan Province.

Since Johan Gunnar Andersson's first excavation and naming, after nearly a century of field archaeological surveys and excavations, thousands of sites of the Yangshao culture or obviously influenced by it have been Discovered, mainly Distributed between Gansu and Henan in the middle reaches of the Yellow River, centered on Guanzhong, western Henan, and southern Shanxi where the tributaries of the Yellow River such as the Wei River, Fen River, and Luo River converge, influencing the marginal areas of Gansu, Qinghai, Hubei, Hebei, and Inner Mongolia.

Due to the large number of sites, they cannot be listed one by one, and only relatively typical ones can be selected for explanation, mainly incluDing the DaDiwan Site in Qin'an, Gansu, the Beishouling Site in baoji and the Banpo site in Xi'an, the jiangzhai site in Lintong, Shaanxi, and the Xishan Site and Dahecun Site in Zhengzhou, Henan.

The DaDiwan Site, located on a low hill on the south bank of the Qingshui River, a tributary of the Wei River, in Wuying township, Qin'an County, Gansu Province, is backed by mountains and facing water.

With an exposed area of 14,752 square meters, it includes five periods: the pre-Yangshao culture period, the early, middle, and late Yangshao culture, and the lower Changshan culture. A total of 240 house sites, 98 stove sites, 325 ash pits and storage pits, 71 tombs, 35 kiln sites, and 12 sections of Ditches from Different periods were cleared.

The east and west parts of the site are Divided into residential areas and burial areas. The residential area has moats on both east and west sides. The houses mostly belong to square or rectangular semi-subterranean builDings, with their backs to the moats and doors Distributed toward the central square.

The early Yangshao house structures include living surfaces, walls, doorways, and stove pits. The living space is generally 20 square meters, with the living surfaces and walls plastered with grass-mixed mud. The doorways are sloped, and the builDing technique of wattle-and-daub walls was not used.

The middle Yangshao period has the largest number of house sites, with more than 100. The house area has expanded, with the largest being more than 60 square meters. The living surfaces are covered with accumulations of red-burnt grass-mud blocks, the roofs are constructed of grass-mud burnt earth, and some houses have adopted wattle-and-daub walls.

The late Yangshao period is mainly built on ground level, with semi-subterranean forms rarely seen. The living surfaces are generally white lime surfaces or jiangshi (caliche) surfaces, and the house columns and column bases have become complex and Diverse, mainly rectangular.

Some large house sites have an area of 270 square meters with an interior area of 150 square meters, grand in scale and possibly belonging to palace-style builDings.

The Beishouling Site, located on the west bank of the Jinling River in baoji city, Shaanxi Province, covers an area of 60,000 square meters. Its early period belongs to the DaDiwan culture, the middle period to the Yangshao Banpo culture, and the late period to the Xiwangcun culture.

A total of 50 house sites, 451 tombs, 75 storage pits, and 4 pottery kilns were Discovered at the site. The houses are centered on a square, Distributed in three groups on the north, west, and south sides, possibly representing three clan tribes of Beishouling.

The houses are square or rectangular semi-subterranean, with doors basically facing the central square, and no surrounDing moat is seen. The ground in some areas of the square is sintered into a hard surface, with post holes and burnt bones remaining, possibly belonging to sacrificial places. The southern half of the site is mainly a burial area.

The tombs are very characteristic, implementing a system of male-male joint burials and female-female joint burials. Most tomb owners face northwest with their feet on the river beach. Many tombs coexist with house site groups in the same period.

Remains such as drainage Ditches were also found, with a large number of pottery, stone tools, and ornaments unearthed.

The Banpo site, located on the east bank of the Chan River in Baqiao District, Xi'an city, Shaanxi Province, is a typical settlement site of the prosperous stage of matrilineal clan commune in the Guanzhong region, belonging to the Neolithic Yangshao culture remains.

The site covers an area of about 50,000 square meters, with an exposed area of 10,000 square meters. A total of 46 house sites, more than 200 storage pits, 6 pottery kilns, 250 tombs, and about 10,000 production and living tools were cleared, as well as remains of millet and rapeseed.

The settlement is slightly irregularly circular, longer from north to south and narrower from east to west. The residential area is in the center, accounting for about 30,000 square meters. There is a small Ditch in the residential area, DiviDing the houses into north and south sections, possibly representing two Different clan communes.

Each section has one large house and several small houses, with doorways basically facing south or southwest. There are storage pits and livestock pens between residential areas. A moat surrounds the residential area.

To the north of the moat is the clan's public cemetery, also interspersed with storage pits, and to the east of the moat is the pottery kiln area.

The houses are circular and square, with two types: semi-subterranean and ground-level builDings, with an area generally around 20 square meters, some small ones only 10 square meters, and large ones up to 160 square meters.

There is a square threshold inside the doorway, and 1-6 columns Directly facing the threshold inside the house to support the roof, adopting the construction method of wattle-and-daub, with living surfaces and walls plastered with grass mud.

The jiangzhai site, located on the north bank of the Lin River in Lintong District, Xi'an city, Shaanxi Province, at the northern foot of Mount Li, is dominated by settlement remains of the Banpo type of the Neolithic Yangshao culture, with a total area of about 50,000 square meters and an exposed area of more than 17,000 square meters.

The village layout is irregularly circular, composed of a square, residential area, kiln area, and burial area, with a large square in the center. Five residential builDing groups are Distributed around the square, possibly representing five Different clan communes, with 120 house sites.

Each group has one large house and several meDium and small houses, facing the central square, forming a grouped ring-column layout centered on the center. There are also storage pits, pottery kilns, livestock pens, and several children's urn burials in the residential area.

The residential area is surrounded by hundreds of meters of artificial moats. To the east of the surrounDing Ditch are three cemeteries of the same period, and to the west of the site near the natural river bank is a pottery kiln area.

The house shapes include circular, oval, square, and irregular, all single-room structures, with three types: subterranean (circular houses), semi-subterranean, and ground-level wooden frame structures. There are post holes inside the houses, with stoves set up. The fire pit faces the doorway, located in the center of the house.

The doorway and interior are separated by a threshold. The living surfaces and walls are all plastered with grass mud and fired, with smooth surfaces. A large number of production tools and living utensils were also found in some houses.

The Xishan Site, located on the terrace on the north bank of the Ku River west of Sunzhuang village, Guxing Town, northern suburb of Zhengzhou city, Henan Province, at the junction of the western Henan hills and the Huang-Huai Plain, covers an area of more than 34,000 square meters and is a high-level settlement of the late Yangshao culture.

The settlement plane is circular, with a Diameter of about 180 meters, and the estimated settlement area is more than 25,000 square meters. There are city walls and city moats.

The existing city wall is 265 meters long, 3-5 meters wide, and 1.75-2.5 meters high, with an inverted trapezoidal foundation trench, and a moat outside the foundation trench. There are two city gates, the north gate and the west gate.

More than 200 house foundations were cleared at the settlement site, which are rectangular or square builDings on ground level. The house groups are laid out accorDing to certain rules and can be Divided into two groups, one with doors facing north and one with doors facing the center of the city.

To the east inside the west gate is a large rammed earth builDing foundation, fan-shaped, about 14 meters long from east to west and 8 meters wide from north to south, surrounded by several house sites, with a large square of several hundred square meters to its north.

More than 2,000 storage pits and ash pits, and 143 tombs and urn burials were found, belonging to two locations, one west of the outside of the city and one north of the inside of the city.

Because the Xishan settlement site has city walls and moats with strong city-wall properties, it is considered the earliest prehistoric city site in the Central Plains region to date.

The Dahecun Site, located on a terrace about 1 kilometer southwest of Dahecun village, northeastern suburb of Zhengzhou city, Henan Province, covers an area of about 300,000 square meters, with an excavation area of more than 7,000 square meters and a cultural accumulation thickness of 7 meters.

The site experienced the matrilineal clan society, patrilineal clan society, and the Xia and Shang periods of slave society. Among them, the remains of Dahecun phases III and IV belong to the late Yangshao culture. More than 50 house sites, nearly 400 storage pits, 354 tombs, and 2 moats from various periods were Discovered.

The settlement is Divided into east and west parts, with an ancient river channel running Diagonally from northeast to southwest.

In the settlement of Dahecun Yangshao culture phase III, except for one semi-subterranean house site, the rest are ground-level builDings, square or trapezoidal in plane, with house areas generally 8-15 square meters, the largest 35 square meters, and the smallest only 2.34 square meters. Most house sites are builDing complexes of two or more rooms.

The house foundations are fired into hard brick-red, with walls full of post holes and traces of reed bundles and horizontal wood. Most houses have square fire platforms. Among them, there is one four-room ground-level house in a row (with an adDitional suite) in the west area, and two two-room ground-level houses in a row in the east area.

Dahecun Yangshao culture phase IV is the transition period from Dahecun to the Longshan culture, with very common remains.

There are 27 house sites, except for 2 semi-subterranean builDings, the rest are ground-level builDings, with varying house areas, the largest more than 100 square meters and the smallest only 1 square meter, mainly rectangular and square single-room meDium-sized houses.

A group of phase IV tombs is Distributed near the west and east residential areas, with the tomb owners' heads facing in opposite Directions in the two areas. This burial form seems to inDicate that there were two Different clan communes at Dahecun.

The prevalence of double-room and multi-room house forms reflects that communal life based on family and clan units gradually became the main form of society at that time.

(4) Longshan culture settlements

The Longshan culture was a Chalcolithic period, a type of cultural remains at the end of the Neolithic Age in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River. It is named after the Chengziya Site first Discovered in 1930 at Longshan Town, Licheng County, Shandong (now belonging to Zhangqiu), dating back 4,500-4,000 years.

The Longshan culture is a very complex composite, involving a wide range, roughly incluDing Henan, Shandong, Shanxi, and Shaanxi in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River. Each region contains many archaeological cultures with regional characteristics, cultural traDitions, and Distribution areas.

For this reason, since the naming of the Longshan culture, accorDing to Different regional cultural features, archaeologists have subDivided it into types such as Shandong Longshan culture, Henan Longshan culture, and Shaanxi Longshan culture.

In terms of artifacts, the most typical feature of the Longshan culture is black pottery, especially eggshell black pottery mainly Distributed in Shandong, characterized by thinness, hardness, luster, and blackness, so the Longshan culture is also called the "Black pottery Culture." In terms of settlements, the most significant feature of the Longshan culture is settlement Differentiation, with settlements Divided into two types: giant settlements and orDinary settlements.

The former generally appear as central settlements, with a certain number of sub-central or orDinary settlements attached around them. Such settlements are generally regarded by the archaeological community as cities, because they reflect relatively strong political and military characteristics.

Some scholars have summarized the new changes in single-site settlements during the Longshan culture period, believing there are at least four aspects of change: first, the upgraDing of settlement surrounDing Ditch scale; second, the upgraDing of settlement moat scale; third, the rise of various city sites, incluDing two types: moat cities and castles; fourth, the increase in the number and scale of double-settlement, multi-settlement sites, and city sites, such as the Haojiatai Site in Yancheng, the Guchengzhai Site in Xinmi, and the Wangchenggang Site in Dengfeng of the Henan Longshan culture, and the Dinggong Site and Yaowangcheng Site of the Shandong Longshan culture.

In terms of settlement nature, most giant settlements during the Longshan culture period already belonged to city-wall type settlements, beyond the category of villages, and strictly speaking do not belong to our Discussion object.

However, to better understand the evolutionary path and change characteristics of prehistoric settlements, it is still necessary to introduce representative and typical city-wall settlements.

The Haojiatai Site, located on the terrace northeast of Shicao Zhao village, east of Yancheng city, Luohe city, Henan Province, has a total area of 65,000 square meters.

The Haojiatai settlement is rectangular in plane, with an area of more than 30,000 square meters, dating back about 4,600 years, and is currently the earliest important city site Discovered archaeologically in the Henan Longshan culture. The east wall, north wall, and four city corners of the settlement city site are relatively well preserved.

There is an 8.8-meter-wide gap in the middle of the east city wall, possibly the location of the city gate. Nearly 30 house sites, more than 500 ash pits, more than 110 tombs, as well as wells, pottery kilns, and ash Ditches were Discovered inside the city. The house sites are located in the southwest of the site, regularly arranged in rows.

The houses were built on elevated earthen platforms, with interior floors higher than exterior, and mostly used adobe for builDing walls, with occasional wattle-and-daub walls.

The row houses face northeast to southwest, with each house having one door on the south wall, with varying door widths between 0.6-0.75 meters, and all exterior doors have thresholds.

The living areas vary in size; for example, the largest room of the Haojiatai phase III culture house site is 18.49 square meters, and the smallest is nearly 9.63 square meters. The interior floors are generally paved with loess, solid and flat.

There are stove sites inside the houses, and daily living utensils were also found, with strong traces of life. The tomb form is rectangular vertical pit earth burial, without burial implements, and most have no grave goods.

The Guchengzhai Site, located around the Guchengzhai villager group, Dafanzhuang village, Quliang township, 35 kilometers southeast of Xinmi city, Henan Province. The site is large in scale, with Neolithic sites inside and outside the city reaching 2.7 million square meters.

The city site was built on a terrace on the east bank of the Zhen River, rectangular in plane, with the existing south, north, and east city walls and two relatively opposite north and south city gate gaps. The three city walls are overall well preserved without any shortage.

There is a 34-90 meter wide moat around the city site, with complete city defense facilities, covering an area of nearly 180,000 square meters, and is a relatively typical city-wall settlement of the Henan Longshan culture era.

The cultural layers of the site include the Yangshao culture, Longshan culture, Erlitou culture, Erligang culture, Yinxu culture, and Han culture, among which the remains from the Longshan culture era are the richest.

A large area of rammed earth builDing complexes from the Longshan culture era was Discovered in the northeast of the city, incluDing two large house sites, one as the main builDing and the other as an auxiliary builDing.

The main builDing should belong to a palace-style builDing, rectangular in plane, facing east from west, 28.4 meters long from north to south and 13.5 meters wide from east to west, with corridors on the south, north, and east sides, covering an area of 383.4 square meters, basically completely preserved, and is a typical early palace-style builDing.

The rammed earth builDing site has 6 rows of post holes or plinths arranged from north to south, DiviDing the house into 7 rooms.

The auxiliary builDing is located to the north of the main builDing, only 7.4 meters apart, composed of three wall foundation trenches, numerous post holes, doorways, and a gatekeeper's room, with a width of 4 meters, belonging to a corridor-style builDing.

AccorDing to relevant research results, these two builDings should be a combination of the main hall and corridor, which is the earliest known large builDing in China with courtyard (siheyuan) characteristics, and it is this architectural pattern that laid the basic pattern of later palace-style builDings in China.

The Dinggong Site, located east of Dinggong village, Changshan Town, Zouping County, Shandong Province, is on the piedmont plain south of the Lubei Plain.

Except for a small amount of Dawenkou culture and Yueshi culture, the cultural layers are mainly Longshan culture, late Shang, and Han culture, with scattered Eastern Zhou and Song dynasty cultural remains.

The site covers an area of about 180,000 square meters, with a total excavation of more than 2,000 square meters, exposing nearly 100 house sites, more than 1,600 ash pits, and nearly 100 tombs from various periods. In adDition, more than 5,000 relics incluDing pottery kilns, wells, and stone, bone, shell, pottery, and bronze artifacts were seen.

Particularly important is the Discovery of Longshan culture pottery fragments suspected to be inscribed with characters. The city site is rounded square in plane, with relatively regular city walls on all sides. The Longshan culture period city wall is about 25 meters wide, and the moat is 30-40 meters wide.

The house sites have two types: semi-subterranean and ground-level, with the latter more numerous. In form, the vast majority are square or rectangular, with circular ones fewer. The former has a smaller area, generally small houses of less than 10 square meters; the latter has a larger area, with the largest exceeDing 50 square meters.

The Yaowangcheng Site, located 16.7 kilometers southwest of Rizhao city, Shandong Province, with its west and south sides close to the Nanxinzhuang River. The site is about 825 meters long from north to south and 630 meters wide from east to west, with a total area of more than 520,000 square meters.

The cultural layer is mainly Longshan culture, incluDing Dawenkou culture, Yueshi culture, Shang-Zhou, and Han cultural remains. House sites, tombs, and pottery, stone, and bone artifacts were unearthed from the site. city walls were Discovered at the site.

The northern city wall runs northwest-southeast, with the main wall about 300 meters long and 26-28 meters wide, with a gap of about 10 meters wide in the middle section, definitely the location of the city gate. A moat with an opening width of nearly 30 meters was found outside the wall, running roughly parallel to the city wall.

The west city wall runs along the edge of the third terrace on the east bank of the Nanxinzhuang River, slightly north by east, with a wall width roughly equivalent to the north wall. The east city wall is basically parallel to the west city wall.

AccorDing to archaeological survey reports, the Yaowangcheng city wall is nearly 500 meters long from north to south and about 300 meters wide from east to west, with the city site area incluDing the city wall being nearly 150,000 square meters.

The house sites have two types: rectangular and circular, with wall foundations, stove sites, and doorways, and the living surfaces are well preserved. The rectangular house sites generally have an area of 12-15 square meters, with doorways located in the south by east.

The walls are 20-25 centimeters thick, with two construction methods: one using rammed earth; the other using adobe staggered masonry, with gaps filled with gray-yellow clay, and finally plastered with yellow mud inside and outside.

The circular house sites have basically the same construction method as rectangular ones, Digging circular foundation trenches on earthen platform bases, with rammed earth and buried columns inside the trenches.

From 1995 to 2004, Shandong University, in collaboration with the University of Pittsburgh, conducted archaeological surveys in the southeastern coastal area of Shandong, concluDing that Yaowangcheng was one of the cores of the southeastern coastal area of Shandong, belonging to a large settlement group stanDing north-south with Liangchengzhen.

II. Major prehistoric settlement sites in the Yangtze River Basin

The Yangtze River Basin refers to the vast area through which the main stream and tributaries of the Yangtze River flow.

The main stream flows through 11 provinces and regions: Qinghai, Tibet, Yunnan, Sichuan, Chongqing, Hubei, Hunan, jiangxi, Anhui, jiangsu, and Shanghai, spanning the abdomen of China; the tributaries extend north and south, involving provinces and regions such as Gansu, Shaanxi, Henan, Guizhou, Guangxi, Guangdong, Fujian, and Zhejiang, with a basin area of 1.8 million square kilometers.

Like the Yellow River Basin, as an area rich in natural geographical resources, the Yangtze River Basin is also a source of the origin and development of Chinese civilization. Not only is agriculture relatively developed, but the settlements formed and changed along with agricultural development are also extremely concentrated and rich.

Compared with the settlement sites in the Yellow River Basin, although the settlements in the Yangtze River Basin show certain similar features in macro appearance due to the consistency of early humans' survival and life demands, after all, the natural geographical conDitions have great Differences, with Different natural environments and climatic conDitions, so there are relatively obvious Differences to a large extent and in micro aspects.

This also fully confirms that the origin of Chinese civilization has been a pattern and cultural characteristic of pluralistic integration since ancient times.

(1) Paleolithic Residential Sites

1. Baise Basin, Guangxi

The Baise Basin is located in the western part of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, spanning Baise city, Tianyang County, and Tiandong County from west to east. The main body of the basin is Distributed northwest-southeast, belonging to a long and narrow basin with a total area of about 800 square kilometers.

The You River traverses the entire basin from west to east. It is precisely because of the pleasant climate, open terrain, and rich natural resources that it is suitable for human habitation and activities, so it has been an important area for human activities since the Paleolithic Age.

The archaeologically Discovered Baise Basin is also the area where Paleolithic sites are most concentrated in Lingnan Guangxi.

Since the first Discovery of Paleolithic sites in the Baise Basin in 1973, more than 100 Paleolithic sites have been Discovered in this area to date, with tens of thousands of Paleolithic artifacts excavated and collected over the years.

The entire Paleolithic site community is mainly Distributed on the high platforms on both banks of the You River in Guangxi, especially in the upper reaches where the terrain is open, the site Distribution is most dense, obviously being the main area of human activity in the Baise Basin.

Some scholars, based on the Distribution of Paleolithic sites, believe that there are at least 4 site clusters and 12 site groups in the Paleolithic sites of the Baise Basin, all showing very obvious artificially organized states.

It is worth noting that among the Paleolithic remains Discovered in the Baise Basin, there is a large batch of typical large cutting tools - hand axes.

These hand axes are similar to the Acheulean stone tools popular in Africa and Eurasia, so the Baise Basin is also regarded by the international academic community as a major area for early human migration and cultural exchange.

In adDition to the Discovery of similar stone tools in the Baise Basin, they have also been found in the Luonan Basin and Liangshan in Hanzhong in the Yellow River Basin.

2. Liyang Plain, Hunan

Since the 20th century, Hunan has Discovered a large number of Paleolithic sites in the four river basins of Xiang, Zi, Yuan, and Li. AccorDing to incomplete statistics, there are more than 300 sites to date, especially concentrated in the western Yuan River basin and the northwestern Li River basin.

The latter is the area most concerned by the academic community, and the sites seen also have certain representativeness and typicality.

The Paleolithic sites in the Li River basin are concentrated in the Liyang Plain in the middle and lower reaches, located on the northwest bank of Dongting Lake in Hunan, surrounded by mountains on the west, south, and north sides.

The climate here is warm and humid, with rich land and water resources and open terrain, suitable for human survival and habitation. Archaeological Discoveries show that at least 500,000 years ago, there were traces of human activities in the Liyang Plain.

The typical site is the Huzhuashan Site in jinshi, where a batch of stone artifacts belonging to the South China gravel stone tool cultural traDition was Discovered, incluDing gravel points. In adDition, sites such as Jigongdang, Wuyashan, and Shiligang were successively Discovered.

The Jigongdang Site is a middle Paleolithic site, and the unearthed stone tools also belong to the southern gravel industry traDition. Contemporary sites include Dashengmiao in Shimen, Zhangjiatan, and Hongqi in Li County.

The cultural age of the Wuyashan Site is in the late Paleolithic, with stone tool assemblages incluDing choppers, hand-axe-like tools, large points, points, scrapers, and stone hammers. Sites of the same nature include Hushan, Huashan, Zhujiashan, and Jinya.

The Shiligang Site is a cultural site of the transition from Paleolithic to Neolithic in the Li River basin, with an area of nearly 40,000 square meters, in which rice phytoliths were also Discovered, which is of great significance for us to explore the origin of agriculture and the origin of human settlements in Hunan.

Roughly 10,000 years ago, the Liyang Plain entered the Neolithic Age. Archaeological Discoveries show that not only Did agriculture originate and develop in this area, but humans also began to enter relatively stable settled life. Typical sites include the Pengtoushan Site and the Bashidang Site.

3. Shuiyang River Basin, Anhui

The Shuiyang River is a tributary on the south bank of the Yangtze River, located in southeastern Anhui Province. Since the 1980s, a large number of Paleolithic sites have been Discovered on both banks of the Shuiyang River, forming a certain community phenomenon.

Representative sites include the Chenshan Site and Guanshan Site in Xuanzhou, and the Maozhushan Site in Ningguo. The Chenshan Site in Xuanzhou was excavated in 1988, covering an area of 100 square meters, with 78 various stone artifacts Discovered.

Surveys suggest that this stone tool site is very large, should be hundreds of thousands of square meters. The Guanshan Site was excavated in 1993, covering an area of about 200 square meters, in which when clearing the upper cultural layer, an ancient human living surface was also Discovered within a 25-square-meter area.

The Maozhushan Site in Ningguo is only 0.5 kilometers from Guanshan, excavated in 1997, with the existing remains area only 3,000 square meters. Among them, a ring composed of 1,167 stone tools with a blank area in the middle was Discovered, which should be a trace of early human life.

The stone tool types include choppers, scrapers, pointed choppers, and stone balls. This series of Discoveries all inDicates that human activities in the Shuiyang River area were relatively frequent and reflected a certain degree of organization.

4. Han River Basin and Yangtze River Coast, Hubei

The middle and lower reaches of the Han River have the jianghan Plain, located in the central and southern part of Hubei Province, starting from Yichang in the west to Wuhan in the east, connected to the Dongting Lake Plain in the south, and is the area with the most concentrated resource elements in Hubei.

The climate here is pleasant, the land is fertile, and water resources are abundant, making it the main area of early human activities in Hubei. AccorDing to archaeological evidence, there are nearly 100 Paleolithic cultural sites Discovered in the Han River basin and along the Yangtze River in Hubei.

Typical ones include the Xuetangliangzi Site in Yun County, the Shilongtou Site, the Huangjiawo Site, the Jigongshan Site, and the Zhangnaodong Site. The Xuetangliangzi Site in Yun County, dating back about 800,000 years, has successively Discovered 2 early human skull fossils and more than 300 stone tools, mainly made of gravel raw materials.

The Shilongtou Site belongs to the early Paleolithic category, roughly equivalent to the Peking Man period, with few stone tool types, mostly choppers.

The Huangjiawo Site, dating back 100,000-50,000 years, belongs to the middle Paleolithic, with an area of about 10,000 square meters and relatively rich stone tool types, incluDing choppers, scrapers, hand picks, hand axes, and notched tools. The Jigongshan Site is a late Paleolithic cultural site, with an area of about 1,000 square meters.

The fact that tens of thousands of stone artifacts and stone materials were unearthed inDicates that the Jigongshan Site may have been a stone tool manufacturing site for early humans.

The irregular blank area composed of several large stone tool assemblages Discovered in the middle of the site may, like the ring remains Discovered at the Maozhushan Site in Ningguo, Anhui, belong to the living surface of early humans.

The Zhangnaodong Site is a rock-shelter cave, a late Paleolithic cultural site, located on the second terrace of the Zhangnao River, Longtan township, Zhongba, Fang County, Hubei, with more than 2,000 stone artifacts Discovered, incluDing choppers, scrapers, and points.

These Paleolithic sites not only inDicate that the Han River basin in Hubei had rich human activities as early as the Paleolithic Age, but also help us understand the origin of settlements in the Yangtze River Basin.

(2) Neolithic settlement sites

Roughly equivalent to the Yellow River Basin, after entering the Neolithic Age, about 10,000 years ago, agriculture began to rise and develop in the Yangtze River Basin, and the residential sites formed since the Paleolithic Age began to develop toward settlement, scale, and density.

As the main area for the origin of rice agriculture, the Yangtze River Basin, due to its fertile land and abundant water resources, achieved relatively good agricultural development.

The rise and development of rice agriculture not only initially solved the food problem of early humans, but also fixed humans within the regional area on the land, making settled life a norm.

Because agriculture Differs from the production and lifestyle of gathering, fishing, and hunting - the former is cultivated on the land, requiring long-term care by humans.

It is precisely due to the long-term demand for agricultural cultivation that sites originally for short-term activities gradually developed into long-term fixed residential sites, which over time became settlements. Overall, the settlement nature of various residential sites in the Neolithic Age began to become increasingly obvious.

However, since agricultural cultivation was still extensive, belonging to the nature of shifting agriculture, residential sites or settlements still had migratory characteristics - that is, when the land resources within a regional area were exhausted, humans had to seek elsewhere to re-establish residential sites or settlements.

The development of early settlements in vast areas of China, incluDing the Yangtze River Basin and the Yellow River Basin, all reflected such characteristics.

To some extent, the rapid development or dense Distribution of settlements was, on one hand, the result of agricultural development and population expansion, and on the other hand, possibly the cause of land resource exhaustion.

This section intends to introduce typical and representative settlement sites within the Yangtze River Basin in conjunction with archaeological excavation materials, in order to better understand the situation and appearance of settlement development and changes in this region.

1. Early Neolithic settlement sites

Archaeological Discoveries of early Neolithic settlement sites in the Yangtze River Basin include the early Neolithic Xianrendong remains and Diaotonghuan cultural remains in Wannian, jiangxi, the Yuchanyan cultural remains in Dao County, Hunan, and the first phase cultural remains of Dingshishan in Yongning, Guangxi.

The middle Neolithic is typified by the Pengtoushan culture type, Zaoshi lower layer culture type, Chengbeixi culture type, and Kuahuqiao culture type.

These cultural types also fully show that after the origin of rice agriculture, after the long development of the early and middle Neolithic Age, it gradually rose to become the main sector of the social economy.

However, compared with after the middle Neolithic, especially the late Neolithic, agricultural development during this period was still limited. Although fixed residential sites or settlement sites all had certain agricultural characteristics, their numbers were not large and the settlement scale was still relatively small.

Nevertheless, from these early human remains, the settlement forms they showed were roughly the same, reflecting that the artificially organized form was becoming increasingly fixed and clan communes began to form.

(1) Xianrendong Remains and Diaotonghuan Cultural Remains in Wannian, jiangxi

The Xianrendong remains and Diaotonghuan remains are two early Neolithic remains, located in a small intermontane basin in the limestone hilly area of Dayuan township, Wannian County, jiangxi Province. The basin is about 4 kilometers long from east to west and 1 kilometer wide from north to south, with the two sites only 800 meters apart.

The Xianrendong remains are a cave site, located at the foot of Xiaohe Mountain in the northern part of the basin, with the cave entrance facing southeast, about 3 meters above the water surface.

The cave entrance is 5.75 meters high and about 18.9 meters wide, with a cave depth of 40 meters, which can be Divided into four branch caves of Different sizes in the north and south. The northern branch cave has a small entrance leaDing to the outside, obviously being a residential site for early human life.

The Diaotonghuan remains are a rock shelter site, located on a small hilltop in the western part of the basin. Because the two are close in Distance, comparable in age, and similar in unearthed artifacts, they are considered to belong to the same ethnic group.

The excavators even believe that the Diaotonghuan Site was a temporary camp and slaughterhouse for the original inhabitants living in Xianrendong to hunt in this area.

After multiple excavations, the Xianrendong Site has Discovered artificial artifacts such as pottery, stone tools, bone tools, and shell tools, as well as animal bones, and more than 20 fire remains and several ash pits. Among them, the Discovery of pottery has attracted extensive attention from the academic community at home and abroad.

Because the invention and use of pottery in prehistoric society largely meant the emergence of agriculture and the beginning of human settled life, the unearthed pottery from Xianrendong dating back 20,000 years can not only explain the transformation of early human production and social behavior, but also inDicate that pottery was manufactured and used 10,000 years or even earlier before the emergence of agriculture.

The Diaotonghuan Site also unearthed the world's earliest wild rice and cultivated rice phytolith specimens. This series of Discoveries all inDicates that humans began to move from the Paleolithic Age to the Neolithic Age, and began the emergence of agriculture and settled life.

(2) Yuchanyan Cave Remains in Dao County, Hunan

The Yuchanyan Cave remains, commonly known as Toad Cave, is located in Baishizhai village, Shouyan Town, Dao County, Hunan Province, and is an early Neolithic remain dating back about 12,000 years. The cave was Discovered in the lower part of a limestone remnant hill, about 5 meters above the ground, with a spacious cave hall at the entrance part.

AccorDing to archaeological excavations, the original landform of Yuchanyan Cave was high in the west and low in the east.

When early humans chose it as a residential address, in order to expand living space for easier habitation and life, they paved gravel on the uneven ground, and in some areas paved gray-white and gray-yellow lime-like accumulations.

In the cave site, burning ash piles and artificial artifacts such as pottery, stone tools, bone tools, horn tools, tooth tools, and shell tools, as well as aquatic and terrestrial animal bones, were Discovered.

These remains are all concentrated in the western part of the cave, which not only inDicates that the west was the main living area for people, but also reflects that early human settlements had preliminary functional zoning.

Among the stone tools, primitive agricultural production tools such as hoe-shaped tools, stone hammers, and sub-waist axe-shaped tools were Discovered.

Among them, the hoe-shaped tool uses a flat and long gravel as raw material, struck into a tool on one end and both sides on a single face, with the using part being the end edge, possibly bound to a curved handle for Digging soil.

The unearthed pottery fragments are also one of the earliest evidence of pottery manufacturing Discovered in China, dating back about 18,000 years. Most importantly, rice husks were Discovered in the cave site. Electron microscope analysis and identification show that these rice husks include both wild rice and artificially cultivated rice.

The Discovery of this series of tools, pottery, and rice remains all inDicates that primitive rice agriculture existed in the Yuchanyan area as early as 10,000 years ago. Of course, it should be pointed out that the existence of agriculture does not mean that early humans fully entered agricultural production and life.

In fact, in early human society represented by Yuchanyan, although agriculture began to appear, people's economic life was still dominated by gathering, fishing, and hunting, supplemented by agriculture.

(3) Pengtoushan Culture Type

Named after its first Discovery at the Pengtoushan Site in Li County, Hunan Province in 1985, the Pengtoushan culture dates back 9,000-8,000 years, mainly located northwest of Dongting Lake in the Yangtze River Basin, concentrated around Dongting Lake and in the lower reaches of the four rivers of Xiang, Zi, Yuan, and Li, especially richest in the Liyang Plain.

The altitude here is generally below 50 meters, with flat terrain, crisscrossing Dikes and embankments, fertile land, and mild climate, suitable for human production, life, and habitation.

Archaeological excavations show that the cultural remains represented by the Pengtoushan Site are currently the earliest known early Neolithic culture in the Dongting Lake area, closely related to the Zaoshi lower layer culture and Chengbeixi culture. Currently, more than 10 Pengtoushan culture sites have been Discovered around Dongting Lake.

In adDition to the Pengtoushan Site, there are the Lijiagang Site, Bashidang Site, Xialiajiawan Site, Xiaojiagang Site, Huangmagang Site, Caojiawan Site in Li County, and the Jinjigang Site in Linli County, among which the Pengtoushan Site and Bashidang Site are the most typical.

The Pengtoushan Site, located on a low slope on the north bank of the Li River about 12 kilometers west of the county seat of Li County, Hunan Province, in the Liyang Plain, covers an area of about 60,000 square meters. The site was Discovered in 1984 and excavated in 1988, with an exposed area of 400 square meters.

Two architectural remains were Discovered, respectively a ground-level builDing with post holes and a small semi-subterranean builDing; 18 tombs were cleared, with small and shallow tomb pits, mostly secondary burials, with pottery grave goods ranging from 1-4 pieces; 15 ash pits were cleared, mostly irregularly circular or oval in plane, with锅底-shaped bottoms.

Among the unearthed relics are artificial artifacts such as stone tools and pottery. Most stone tools are chipped stone tools, while pottery is simple and primitive in manufacture, made by the primitive coiling method, with charcoal fragments mixed in the pottery body.

AccorDing to observations by archaeological excavators, the pottery fragments from the site also contain a large amount of carbonized rice husks and grains.

From the chipped stone tools, polished stone axes, complete buffalo bones, and rice remains Discovered at the Pengtoushan Site, the economic life of Pengtoushan began to transition from gathering, fishing, and hunting to agricultural production, but still dominated by the former, with a certain scale of rice cultivation and livestock breeDing.

The Bashidang Site, located in Wufu village, Mengxi Town, about 20 kilometers north of the county seat of Li County, Hunan Province, on the slope on the north bank of the Cen River, a tributary of the Li River, slopes from northwest to southeast, covering an area of about 30,000 square meters, with an excavation area of more than 1,200 square meters.

A large number of relics from the Pengtoushan culture period were Discovered at the site, incluDing pottery, stone tools, bone tools, wood tools, and more than 100 types of plant and fruit pit remains. In adDition, tens of thousands of complete carbonized rice grains and rice were unearthed.

After detection and identification by agricultural experts, they are considered to be rice with characteristics of both inDica, japonica, and wild rice, being primitive ancient cultivated rice of small-grained inDica type in the Differentiation period.

The north side of the settlement uses a section of ancient river channel as a protective enclosure, with earthen walls and moats surrounDing the east, south, and west sides, forming a closed irregular rectangular living area, reflecting a certain degree of planning and defensiveness.

The earthen wall and moat are the most important Discoveries at the site. This site is currently the earliest early settlement with moats and earthen walls Discovered archaeologically in China. Its Discovery has important academic value for us to understand the external form and economic and social forms of early settlements.

More than 10 houses were Discovered at the site, incluDing semi-subterranean builDings, but most are rectangular or square ground-level builDings, incluDing stilt-style (ganlan) and platform-style. There are stove pits inside the houses, with strong traces of life.

More than 100 tombs are scattered around the residential area, without a deDicated burial area, with pottery grave goods in the tombs. The Discovery of this settlement site inDicates that settlements with moats and earthen walls in the Yangtze River Basin had already formed in the early Neolithic Age and had a certain scale.

(4) Zaoshi Lower Layer Culture Type

The Zaoshi lower layer culture is named after the excavation of the Zaoshi Site in Shimen, Hunan Province. The Zaoshi Site was first Discovered in the early 1960s, but was initially only considered a Shang dynasty site.

Later, with two excavations in 1977 and 1981, exposing an area of 1,100 square meters, and the Discovery of Neolithic cultural remains Different from the early Daxi culture remains in this region in the lower layer of the site, it attracted the attention of the archaeological community.

Archaeologists speculated that this might represent a new "culture." Later, with the successive Discovery of same-type cultural remains, the archaeological community formally proposed the name of this culture type.

Like the Pengtoushan culture, the Zaoshi lower layer culture is mainly Distributed around the Dongting Lake area, but comparatively, its Distribution area is wider, incluDing not only the lower reaches of the four rivers of Xiang, Zi, Yuan, and Li, but also extenDing to the middle reaches, especially concentrated on the north bank of the Li River within Li County and Linli County.

Currently, more than 30 Zaoshi lower layer culture sites have been Discovered in this area, spread over eight or nine counties and cities around Dongting Lake. Among them, sites with obvious settlement characteristics include the Hujiawuchang Site and Fenshanbao Site.

The Hujiawuchang Site, located in the northwest of Linli County, Hunan Province, north of the Li River, at the western edge of the Dongting Lake Plain, covers an area of more than 7,000 square meters. It was first excavated in 1986, exposing an area of 160 square meters, basically square in plane.

Two red-burnt earth houses were Discovered at the site. The houses are rectangular ground-level builDings with doorways and post holes, possibly with columns set up to support the interior roof; the houses have a certain height and the interior is relatively spacious.

There is also one tomb, with chipped and polished stone tools unearthed, as well as a large number of Distinctive pottery. The pottery is made by the clay-slab coiling method. Except for a very small amount of coarse clay red pottery and black pottery, the exterior of the pottery has a thin and delicate red pottery skin.

The forms include ring-footed plates, double-eared jars, high-necked jars, and plate-mouthed jars. Plain-surfaced pottery accounts for a certain proportion, but most have simple decorations such as incised patterns, cord patterns, stamped patterns, impressed patterns, and applique patterns.
