The Discovery of these remains inDicates that early human production and life underwent significant changes, not only accumulating relatively rich survival and life experience, but also further enhancing aesthetic consciousness.

The Fenshanbao Site, located at Qianlianghu Farm, 35 kilometers west of Yueyang city, Hunan Province, on a low and gentle small terrace in the lake and marsh area of East Dongting Lake.

The site was Discovered during the 1985 cultural relics survey, with an area of more than 40,000 square meters, and was excavated in 1990, exposing an area of 149 square meters. Remains such as residential sites, ash pits, and tombs, as well as a large number of relics, were Discovered at the site.

The house sites are similar in form, nearly rectangular in plane, with house foundations roughly north-south oriented, and well-preserved living surfaces, generally with similarly formed fire pits. The fire pit is located in the southeast corner, circular, and the excavators believe that the fire pits seen at the site may be unrelated to Diet.

The stone tools include choppers, stone Discs, scrapers, burins, stone axes, and whetstones by form.

The unearthed pottery is all hand-made, uneven in thickness, with coiling traces, mainly charcoal-tempered red pottery, generally decorated with red slip, with a surface layer, and the walls are mostly polished, with decorations, mainly simple geometric patterns; the main vessel types include jars, ring-footed plates, and bowls, in large quantities and Diverse forms.

In terms of cultural relations, the Fenshanbao Site has a certain relationship with the Hujiawuchang Site, with roughly comparable ages, and also has some connection with the Chengbeixi culture, but there are also Differences, reflecting the characteristics of unity and Diversity of early human culture.

(5) Chengbeixi Culture Type

The Chengbeixi culture is named after its first Discovery at the Chengbeixi Site in Yidu, Hubei Province. The Chengbeixi Site was Discovered in 1973 and excavated twice in 1983 and 1984.

In adDition to Discovering that the upper layer is Shang dynasty cultural accumulation, the lower layer is a Neolithic cultural layer, which is Different from contemporary cultures Discovered in the same regional area.

With the increase of same-type archaeological Discoveries, archaeologists proposed the naming of "Chengbeixi culture." Among the Neolithic cultural remains in Hubei, the Chengbeixi culture has the earliest age, from 6500 BCE to 5000 BCE.

This type of culture is mainly Distributed in the hilly zone between the western Hubei mountains and the jianghan Plain, that is, along the Yangtze River between the eastern part of the Three Gorges and the jianghan Plain.

Although this regional area has many high mountains and gorges, the gorges are relatively wide, with gently sloping hills on both banks of the Yangtze River, good soil quality in front of the mountains, and large-area terraces, suitable for human survival and habitation.

To date, more than 10 Chengbeixi culture type sites have been Discovered archaeologically. The Chengbeixi Site is representative of rich cultural relics, but most sites incluDing it have not Discovered house sites.

However, if the clustering characteristic of houses is used as a main criterion for judging settlement formation, then there are not many sites with settlement characteristics in the Chengbeixi culture type. Although some sites have cleared house sites, there are only 1-2 of them.

For example, the ChayuanDian Site Discovered 2 house foundations, and the Wangjiadu Site Discovered 1, neither with strong settlement nature.

Although many sites have unearthed rich pottery, stone tools, and other remains, reflecting frequent early human activities in this regional area, after all, a settlement is a regional space where material entity space and non-material social space highly overlap, a social unit with relatively clear boundaries.

Therefore, many sites seen in the Chengbeixi culture type cannot strictly be attributed to the category of settlements.

(6) Kuahuqiao Culture Type

The Kuahuqiao culture is named after the excavation of the Kuahuqiao Site in Xianghu village, Xiaoshan District, Hangzhou city, Zhejiang Province, dating back 8,000-7,000 years.

The Kuahuqiao Site is located on the shore of Xianghu in the southwestern part of Xiaoshan, south of Kuahuqiao, with low hills on both north and south sides, covering an area of more than 30,000 square meters, with an exposed area of more than 1,000 square meters.

Four ruined house sites, more than 20 ash pits, and one tomb were Discovered at the site.

One identifiable house is a rectangular ground-level builDing, with remaining walls 30-40 centimeters high and 35 centimeters wide, the walls built of gray-white soil with wooden stakes buried in the middle, and burnt earth surfaces remaining inside; among them, there is a square ash pit with a "well"-shaped wooden frame, preserving a whole pit of acorns.

The unearthed relics include artificial artifacts such as pottery, stone tools, bone tools, and wood tools, as well as animal bones, plant stems and branches, and more than 1,000 carbonized rice grains, rice, and rice husks, and a dugout canoe.

Most pottery is daily utensils, with forms incluDing cauldrons, round-bottomed jars, double-eared jars, straight-mouthed bowls, ring-footed plates, and ring-footed bowls, among which double-eared jars and ring-footed plates belong to painted pottery.

pottery spinning wheels and thread wheels were also seen, the latter still attached with fibrous thread ends. The stone tools are all polished, mainly incluDing axes, adzes, chisels, hammers, grinDing stones, and grinDing sticks, with relatively exquisite manufacture and fully polished surfaces.

The bone and horn tools are mainly agricultural, fishing-hunting, textile, sewing, and living utensils, such as plows, arrowheads, harpoons, awls, needles, daggers, spoons, whistles, and forks.

Wood tools are also mostly used for fishing-hunting, textile, construction, and production tools, the most typical being dugout canoes, shovels, paddles, ladders, dustpans, and wooden bows.

This series of Discoveries all inDicates that the Kuahuqiao people had primitive rice agriculture, but obviously also had an economic life of gathering, fishing, and hunting.

However, from the large number of agricultural production tools and rice remains unearthed, agriculture may have risen to a dominant position in the economic life of the Kuahuqiao people. We can consider the Kuahuqiao Site an early settlement with relatively obvious agricultural characteristics.

Its production and life were not only very active but also extremely rich, reflecting that the economic form and social structure of early humans in the lower Yangtze River region underwent certain changes.

It can be affirmed that as an early Neolithic cultural remain in the lower Yangtze River region, the Discovery of Kuahuqiao is of great significance for us to understand the early settlement origin and forms in this regional area.

The Zoumaling-Tunzishan Site: Zoumaling is located in Dongsheng Town, Shishou city, Hubei Province, and is a late Neolithic settlement site. The site is located along the Yangtze River, only 4 kilometers north of the Yangtze River, belonging to the transition zone from low hills to plains, with a superior geographical location.

The site is irregularly rectangular in plane, with a total area of about 80,000 square meters and an excavation area of 1,200 square meters. Tunzishan is located on a low hill only 50 meters northeast of Zoumaling but connected to it, with an area roughly equivalent to Zoumaling.

It has not been excavated yet, but archaeological surveys have found large areas of red-burnt earth house site-type accumulations. Surveys found that Zoumaling-Tunzishan should be a double city site. Because surveys found city moats and walls enclosing both accorDing to the terrain, the site obviously presents an irregular "8" shape.

Archaeological surveys also found that settlement sites of Different scales exist around the double city site, reflecting that the double city site may be the central settlement in this regional area.

From the excavation situation of Zoumaling, a total of 4 house sites, 2 pottery kilns, 109 ash pits were Discovered, 19 tombs were cleared, and the unearthed relics are very rich.

The phase I house sites are rectangular ground-level builDings with foundation trenches, wooden columns supporting grass-mixed mud walls, with living surfaces rammed and trimmed, facing south.

There is 1 phase II house site, a single-room house site, irregularly rectangular, with an area of about 8 square meters, composed of post holes, thresholds, and living surfaces, with the living surface being gray-white clay with hard soil quality. No house sites were found in phase III.

The phase IV house site is a crank-shaped multi-room ground-level builDing with wattle-and-daub walls. The west side is a large room, and the east side is two or more small rooms, with an 85-centimeter-wide doorway between the large and small rooms.

The small room is located east of the house site, and 4 pottery vessels inverted on the living surface were Discovered in its northwest corner: a dou (stemmed vessel), jar, bowl, and cup; there are 2 ash layers, and the small room may belong to a kitchen or Dining place.

A large number of pottery fragments were found inside the house site, and 17 spinning wheels and 8 stone tools were also seen, incluDing 6 stone axes.

(2) Qujialing Culture settlements

The Qujialing culture is named after its first Discovery at the Qujialing Site in Jingshan County, Hubei Province, dating back 5,500-4,600 years, succeeDing the late Daxi culture and preceDing the early Shijiahe culture.

The Qujialing Site is located between two small rivers, the Qingmudang River and its tributary the Qingmu River, at the southern foot of Dahong Mountain, situated on an oval-shaped mound with gentle terrain, covering an area of about 400,000 square meters, with an exposed area of nearly 1,000 square meters.

The site has Discovered ash pits, tombs, and 2 large-area red-burnt earth remains, as well as Distinctive pottery, incluDing painted pottery, painted-decorated pottery, and painted pottery spinning wheels.

The Distribution of the Qujialing culture is centered on the jianghan Plain in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, extenDing northward across the Tongbai Mountains to the Nanyang Basin in southwestern Henan, with cultural influence reaching central Henan and even the banks of the Yellow River, northwestward along the Han River to the Wudang Mountain area; westward Directly to the Three Gorges; southward enDing at the southern bank of Dongting Lake, with influence reaching central Hunan; eastward to the Huanggang and Huangshi area, bounded by the Dabie Mountains to the northeast.

This culture spans the three provinces of Hubei, Hunan, and Henan. To date, archaeology has Discovered nearly 1,000 sites in this regional area, and we only select one or two important ones for introduction.

The Jimingcheng Site, located at the junction of Longchuanzui village and Wangjiachang village, Shizikou Town, Gongan County, Jingzhou city, Hubei Province, sits on a narrow plain, only 2 kilometers south of a river, located in the connecting zone between the jianghan Plain and the Dongting Lake Plain.

Jimingcheng is irregularly oval in plane, slightly trenDing from northeast to southwest, with obvious turns at the southeast and southwest corners. The maximum north-south Distance is about 500 meters, east-west about 400 meters, with an area of about 150,000 square meters. The city site is well preserved, with only the northeast part missing.

The city wall has a perimeter of about 1,100 meters, with a top width of about 15 meters and a bottom width of about 30 meters. There is a moat outside the city wall, with a perimeter of about 1,300 meters. Three city gate remains were Discovered at the site, namely the east gate, west gate, and north gate.

The east gate is about 12 meters wide; the west gate is located south of the west city wall, 11-12 meters wide; the north gate is located west of the city wall, 14 meters wide. Cultural relics such as pottery were also unearthed from the city site.

This site is of great significance for us to understand the social development level and early settlement forms in the jianghan region.

The Jijiaocheng Site, belonging to the middle Qujialing culture, is located in Cennan township, about 12 kilometers north of Li County, Hunan Province, in the central Liyang Plain.

The settlement site is nearly square in plane, with rounded corners, 400 meters long from east to west and about 370 meters wide from north to south, covering an area of nearly 150,000 square meters, with an exposed area of 190 square meters. The west and north city walls are well preserved.

The southern section of the west wall is about 60 meters wide, with a residual height of 4-5 meters; the western section of the north wall is 40-60 meters wide, with a residual height of 2-3 meters, with a gap in the middle of the north wall, possibly the location of the city gate; the east wall only retains the northern and southern sections, about 40 meters wide, with a residual height of 3-4 meters; the south wall has been destroyed.

Jijiaocheng has moats and a city moat. A conical earthen platform was Discovered at the site, with a bottom Diameter of nearly 10 meters and a height of about 1.5 meters.

In the center of the platform top, there is a red-burnt earth pile about 2.5 meters in Diameter and about 1 meter thick, level with the top surface of the platform, with a large amount of broken pottery fragments remaining, located under the city wall, possibly related to sacrificial activities held during city wall construction, roughly belonging to the late Qujialing culture.

Archaeological excavations also show that the construction of the Jijiaocheng city site was continuous, experiencing several stages: middle Qujialing culture, late Qujialing culture, and early Shijiahe culture, inDicating that this was an early settlement with a large time span and continuous use.

Moreover, a settlement community formed around Jijiaocheng, with nearly 40 settlements closely clustered within an area of only 20 square kilometers, reflecting an obvious trend of geopolitical integration.

These Discoveries inDicate that Jijiaocheng, as a regional central settlement, already had the role and significance of geopolitical integration.

The Huanglianshu Site, also known as the Longshangang Site, is located on a sloping terrace west of Huanglianshu village, Taohe township, Xichuan County, Henan Province, backed by a 50-meter-high earthen mound to the southeast and adjacent to the Huangling River to the northwest, at the confluence of the Dan River and Huangling River.

The existing area of the site is about 200,000 square meters, with the Neolithic remains accumulation range about 140,000 square meters, and cultural accumulation thickness of 1-4.2 meters, incluDing remains from the Neolithic Age, Western Zhou, Han, Song-Yuan, Ming-Qing periods, dominated by Neolithic remains, containing remains from the Yangshao culture, Qujialing culture, and Shijiahe culture periods.

Among them, the Qujialing culture lasted the longest and had the richest relics. There are 25 house foundations, mostly located on the terrace in the southeast of the site, backed by mountains and facing water, facing the Huangling River in front and relying on the loess mound behind.

The houses are in a courtyard layout, Divided into north and east rows of houses.

The north row of houses is northwest-southeast oriented, basically parallel short row houses, with 5 house sites; the east row of houses is northeast-southwest oriented, longituDinally long row houses, with 17 house sites; three small courtyard-style open squares are formed in the middle, with a single large room in the south-central part of the courtyard, with the door facing northeast, possibly the residence of the clan leader or a space for public activities.

These houses are Divided into single-room and double-room types, among which 8 are double-room and the rest are single-room; the houses are neatly arranged with close spacing, some spacing between 0.3-1.2 meters; the house shape is square or rectangular, dug and built wattle-and-daub builDings, with walls plastered with white lime; there are fire pits, generally one per room; a few houses have white lime floors outside.

There are 17 ash pits and 38 tombs, with few grave goods in the tombs, only 4 tombs respectively with one or two pieces of pottery (Ding tripods, jars) and rough ornaments, mainly earrings composed of stone beads and pottery rings, stone bracelets, and stone ornaments.

Although there are few grave goods, they still reflect that society began to Differentiate, possibly with Distinctions in status and wealth.

The settlement site unearthed 997 production tools and living utensils, the former such as stone axes, stone adzes, stone sickles, stone knives, stone net sinkers, pottery spinning wheels, bone fishhooks, arrowheads, bone awls, horn awls, tooth awls, bone needles, stone mortars and pestles, pottery pestles, and grinDing tools; the latter incluDing pottery Ding tripods, pottery jars, pottery bowls, pottery vats, pottery basins, and pottery pots.

These Discoveries all inDicate that Huanglianshu was a large settlement with strict social organization and frequent social activities.

(3) Hemudu culture settlements

The Hemudu culture is named after its first Discovery in Hemudu Town, Yuyao city, Zhejiang Province. It is a late Neolithic culture in the area south of the lower reaches of the Yangtze River, dating back 7,000-5,300 years.

Archaeological Discoveries show that the Hemudu culture is mainly Distributed in the Ningbo-Shaoxing Plain on the south bank of Hangzhou Bay and the Zhoushan Islands.

Currently, relatively clear Hemudu culture sites, in adDition to the Hemudu site in Yuyao, include Xiangjiashan, Zhushan, Xiazhuang in Yuyao, Tongjia'ao in Cixi, Baziqiao and Shaxi in Ningbo, Tashan in Xiangshan, Mingshanhou in Fenghua, and Baiquan in Dinghai, with the Hemudu site being the most typical.

The Hemudu site, located on a narrow river valley plain on the south bank of Hangzhou Bay, is a transition zone from hills to plains, with terrain gently sloping from southwest to northeast, with Siming Mountain to the south, Cinan Mountain area to the north, and north-south trenDing low hills to the east.

The excavation area of the site is 2,630 square meters, with a total of more than 1,000 wooden components unearthed, incluDing three types: long round logs, pile wood, and wooden boards.

Thirteen rows of orderly arranged pile wood were Discovered at the site, possibly with more than 6 builDings, among which one connected long house has a depth of about 7 meters, with a 1.3-meter-wide front porch under the eaves, and a width of more than 23 meters.

The house remains are mainly arranged in rows, with pile wood driven into the virgin soil, and scattered beams, column logs, and thick boards also seen, with no grass reinforcement or red-burnt earth, all being mortise-and-tenon wooden structures, typical stilt-style (ganlan) builDings.

The important components of the wooden builDing remains are basically northwest-southeast oriented, some nearly north-south, obviously arranged with backs to mountains and faces to water.

From the architectural structure, it is clearly Different from the semi-subterranean or ground-level builDings in the Yellow River Basin, and the construction techniques are also Different. In adDition to Differences in social organization structure, this is more likely caused by Different natural geographical environments.

There are 27 tombs, located in the west, north, and northeast of the excavation area.

In the first cultural layer, the maximum number of grave goods is 5-6 pieces, with the minimum only 1 piece, mostly pottery, generally with cauldrons and dou vessels, as well as jade and stone; no grave goods were seen in the second cultural layer; in the third cultural layer, no tomb pits are seen, no burial implements, the vast majority have no grave goods, and a few have a small amount of grave goods.

One wooden well was Discovered, composed of more than 200 pile woods and long round logs, with a circle of nearly circular fence piles on the periphery, about 6 meters in Diameter and about 28 square meters in area, and a square vertical shaft on the elevation.

Archaeology shows that the animal bones at Hemudu involve 47 species of animals; most test pits have found 20-50 centimeter thick accumulation layers of rice, rice husks, rice leaves, rice stems mixed with wood chips and weaves. After identification, the rice belongs to artificially cultivated rice.

Accompanying the rice remains, a large number of agricultural tools were also unearthed, mainly bone plows (bone si), as many as 170 pieces, among which 2 pieces still have wooden handles and rattan for binDing remaining on the handle.

These Discoveries inDicate that rice agriculture had not only risen to become the main economic sector of the Hemudu people, but also that rice cultivation had entered the "plow cultivation stage." Moreover, from nearly 10 types of bone textile tools incluDing spinning wheels, yarn winDing rods, warp DiviDing wood, warp beams, machine knives, shuttle-shaped tools, and bone needles, as well as thousands of production and living tools such as stone tools, pottery, and wood tools, the Hemudu people had a relatively developed agricultural economy, while also having livestock and hunting economic activities, reflecting the social structure and development degree of clan communes in the late Neolithic Age of the Yangtze River Basin.

(4) Majiabang Culture settlements

The Majiabang culture is an archaeological culture represented by the Discovery and excavation of the Majiabang Site in Tiandaiqiao village, Nanhu District, jiaxing city, Zhejiang Province.

It is a late Neolithic culture in the lower Yangtze River region, mainly Distributed in the Taihu Lake surrounDing area of southern jiangsu and northern Zhejiang.

Currently, there are more than 30 excavated Majiabang culture sites, mainly incluDing the Majiabang Site, Luojiajiao Site in Tongxiang, Chuodun Site in Kunshan, and Luotuodun Site in Yixing, among which the Majiabang Site and Luojiajiao Site are the most typical.

The Majiabang Site, located 7.5 kilometers southwest of the city center of jiaxing, sits on a plain where three rivers intersect, with the site about 150 meters long from east to west and 100 meters wide from north to south, covering an area of 15,000 square meters, with an excavation area of 213 square meters.

One rectangular house site was Discovered in the upper cultural layer, with 13 post holes on the east, south, and west sides, and a gate site at the southeast corner. Within the post hole range, there is a layer of yellow-green hard soil surface about 8 centimeters thick, which should be the living surface. Bone arrowheads, bone chisels, etc.

were unearthed around the house. A house suspected of being burned was also seen. The lower layer architectural remains are simple, being a pit, with cattle and deer bones Discovered, not necessarily residential builDings.

The west and northwest of the site are burial grounds, more than 10 meters from the residential area, with 30 skeletons Discovered, no tomb pits. Artificial artifacts such as bone tools, stone tools, jade artifacts, and pottery were unearthed.

The bone tools are mostly production tools such as bone awls, bone arrowheads, bone chisels, and bone needles, and the stone tools are also tools such as stone adzes and stone axes.

The Luojiajiao Site, located northeast of Shimen Town, Tongxiang city, Zhejiang Province, is about 400 meters long from east to west and 300 meters wide from north to south, with a total area of about 120,000 square meters and an exposed area of 1,338 square meters.

53 ash pits were cleared, with rich archaeological relics and animal and plant remains Discovered. The unearthed relics include about 800 complete or restorable pottery, stone, bone, and wood artifacts.

Among them, pottery includes daily utensils such as cauldrons, basins, plates, bowls, dou vessels, Ding tripods, and pots, as well as spinning wheels; stone tools include axes, adzes, knives, and spinning wheels; bone tools are mainly production tools such as arrowheads, plows, and daggers; among the wood tools, there is a batch of squarely processed mortise-and-tenon wooden builDing components, with processing methods incluDing fire roasting and axe and adze chiseling.

Some wooden components have pin holes on the tenons, and the mortises are Divided into penetrating and non-penetrating, all made accorDing to Different builDing needs, aiming to make the wooden components more firmly joined. These Discoveries all inDicate that wooden builDings generally existed at the Luojiajiao Site.

(5) Shijiahe Culture settlements

The Shijiahe culture is named after the Discovery and confirmation of the Shijiahe Site Group in Tianmen city, Hubei Province, and is a late Neolithic culture type in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River following the Qujialing culture.

The Distribution area of the Shijiahe culture is roughly equivalent to that of the Qujialing culture, mainly Distributed in the area centered on the central jianghan Plain of Hubei and its surrounDing range, with raDiation scope incluDing Hubei, southwestern Henan, and northern Hunan, even reaching the Zhengzhou-Luoyang area to the north.

To date, archaeology has Discovered nearly 1,000 Shijiahe culture sites, especially forming a Shijiahe site group around the Shijiahe Town area of Tianmen.

The Shijiahe Site Group, located about 17 kilometers northwest of Tianmen city, Hubei Province, is in the ridge-shaped plain area of the low hills south of Dahong Mountain, at the confluence of the Shijia River in the east and the Maxi River in the southwest.

The site group has more than 30 sites, densely Distributed north of Shijiahe Town at altitudes between 30-45 meters. Outside this range, sites are only sporaDically Distributed, fully reflecting the community nature of the Shijiahe site group.

AccorDing to archaeological excavations, a "Shijiahe earthen city" was Discovered in the area centered on Tanjialing, incluDing sites such as Dengjiawan, Sanfangwan, Tucheng, Huangjinling, and Yangjiawan.

The earthen city is located east of Dengjiawan and north of Huangjinling, with residential houses in the north and west of the city and the southwest end outside the city.

The earthen city is slightly shoe-shaped in plane, about 510 meters long from north to south and 280 meters at its widest from east to west, covering an area of nearly 1.2 million square meters, with low gullies resembling ring-shaped moats around the city wall.

The east and north sections of the city wall are slightly wider, with larger height Differences, and the city circle is very complete. There is a gap about 12 meters wide at the north of the east section, possibly the location of the city gate.

A large number of mid-late Western Zhou remains were also Discovered in the city site, inDicating that the city site may have been in continuous use for a long time.

Outside the city site, there are small-scale sites scattered around the city, such as Hujiawan, Zhoujiawan, Yanjia Xinchang, and Yanjia Guangling to the north of the city, Kubaishu, Tanjiagang, and Yandouziwan to the west of the city, and Maojialing, Wangjiatai, Aojiaquan, and Zhaguofentou to the northeast of the city.

This Distribution seems to inDicate a master-suborDinate relationship between the earthen city and surrounDing settlements, with the earthen city being the political power core and surrounDing settlements suborDinate to this core.

It can be seen that the Shijiahe site group is undoubtedly a geopolitically integrated settlement community with the earthen city as the central settlement.

(6) Liangzhu culture settlements

The Liangzhu culture is represented by the Discovery and excavation of the Liangzhu site in Yuyao city, Zhejiang Province, dating back 5,300-4,500 years, and is a late Neolithic culture type in the lower Yangtze River region.

Archaeological Discoveries show that the Liangzhu culture is mainly Distributed in the surrounDing areas of the Qiantang River basin and Taihu Lake basin, especially dense in the northeast and east of the Qiantang River basin.

AccorDing to relevant data, there are more than 200 Liangzhu culture sites reported to date, and some scholars estimate even no less than 1,000, such as Fanshan and Yaoshan in Yuhang, Zhejiang, as well as Zhaolingshan in Kunshan, jiangsu, Caoxieshan in Wuxian, Sidun in Wujin, and Fuquanshan in Qingpu, Shanghai.

Among the Discovered sites, those with the clearest settlement attributes and certain clustering characteristics are mainly the Liangzhu culture site group in Yuhang, Zhejiang.

The Liangzhu culture site group, located in the northern suburb of Hangzhou city, Zhejiang Province, is mainly Distributed in the three towns of Pingyao, Anxi, and Liangzhu in Yuhang city, covering an area of about 34 square kilometers.

The site group is located in the border zone between the western Zhejiang mountainous hills and the Hangzhou-jiaxing-Huzhou Plain, being a hilly valley with dense water networks. To date, more than 100 sites of pure Liangzhu culture and sites containing Liangzhu culture have been Discovered in this area.

Overall, the Liangzhu culture site group can be roughly Divided into three areas: first, about 30 northern sites, with the narrow zone between the north bank of the East Tiao Stream and the remnants of Tianmu Mountain as the main Distribution range, concentrated at the foot of the southern slope of Dazhe Mountain hills and the piedmont zone, Distributed in two parallel belts; second, the area centered on Mojiaoshan in the southwest of the site group, with more than 50 sites Distributed; third, the area centered on Xunshan in Liangzhu Town in the southeast, with more than 20 sites Distributed within a 1-kilometer raDius, very dense.

The types of remains and relics Discovered in the site group are very rich, incluDing remains such as residential sites, cemeteries, altars, and hanDicraft workshops, as well as relics such as production and living tools and sacrificial vessels.

The residential sites of the site group are Divided by scale, represented by three sites respectively: Mojiaoshan, Yaojiadun, and Miaoqian. Mojiaoshan is a giant rectangular rammed earth platform with an area exceeDing 30,000 square meters, with three small mounds on the site, possibly the remains of the main builDing.

Within a 100-square-meter area on the south side, several rows of large column pits were Discovered, possibly ritual builDings.

Later, in the southeast of the site, not only large-area pit-shaped burnt earth accumulations were cleared, but also remains such as neatly arranged Ditch ridges, stone accumulation pits, and ash pits filled with pure soil were exposed. These Discoveries all reflect that the Mojiaoshan Site may be a central settlement site.
