The road surface is hard, gray-brown, 0.02-0.03 meters thick, and the roadbed is 0.15-0.20 meters thick. The road surface soil is dense with mixed flowers, and should have been flat-rammed or rolled during road construction.

AccorDing to archaeological report speculation, the ancient road Discovered at the Nanliangdu Site may be a branch of the Han dynasty post road. Combined with the unearthed remains, no obvious traces of agricultural production activities were found.

From this, the Nanliangdu settlement site does not seem to be an agricultural settlement, but a transportation-type scattered residence site.

The Yongnian Yulin Site, located west of Yulin village, Yongnian County, Hebei. The site is about 1,500 meters south of the Ming River, located in the southern Hebei plain, with flat terrain. The total excavation area is 2,000 square meters, with cultural remains from three periods: Neolithic, Western Zhou, and Han dynasty.

The cultural layer accumulations of the Neolithic and Western Zhou periods are relatively thin, inDicating that the scale of human activities here in these two periods should not be large. Different from this, the Han dynasty period remains are relatively rich, and there should have been large-scale production and life activities.

Therefore, the Yulin Site is a Han dynasty settlement site dominated by Han dynasty remains. From the clearing situation, Han dynasty remains include ash pits, wells, and ash Ditches.

The ash pits have three shapes: circular, oval, and irregular, with pottery fragments and brick and tile fragments unearthed in the pits; 2 wells, with the well mouth circular in plane, 0.8 meters in Diameter, 5.46 meters deep, and the well wall built of green bricks.

The site unearthed iron production tools such as plowshares, hoes, shovels, and chisels, and pottery living utensils such as pots, cauldrons, basins, urns, and boshanlu censers, and also saw architectural pottery such as tile ends and flat tiles, and several Wuzhu coins.

A large number of daily utensils and architectural components such as tile ends and flat tiles inDicate that the Yulin Site is a village site, and should be a typical agricultural village.

(3) village Sites in Henan Region

Henan gets its name because most of it is located south of the Yellow River. Situated in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, it borders Hebei and Shanxi to the north, Shandong to the northeast, Anhui to the southeast, Shaanxi to the northwest, and Hubei to the southwest, belonging to the central-eastern region of China.

Henan's terrain is high in the west and low in the east, with the Taihang Mountains, Funiu Mountains, Tongbai Mountains, and Dabie Mountains surrounDing the north, west, and south, while the central, eastern, and northern parts are the North China Plain, flat and open, with mountains and hills in the southwest and the Dabie mountain area in the southeast.

As the main birthplace of the Chinese nation and Chinese civilization, Henan had ape-man activities as early as 45 million years ago, and in the Stone Age had rich traces of human activities, incluDing the Xiaonanhai culture and Lingjing culture of the Paleolithic Age, and the jiahu culture, Peiligang culture, Henan Yangshao culture, and Longshan culture of the Neolithic Age.

After the Erlitou culture, Henan entered the Chalcolithic age and produced the first dynasty in Chinese history - the Xia dynasty.

Thereafter, through the Shang, Western Zhou, and Eastern Han, up to the Song dynasty, more than 20 dynasties successively established or moved their capitals here, and this place was long the center of Chinese politics, economy, culture, and transportation hub.

Precisely because Henan has been the main region of human activities in China since prehistoric society, there are relatively many archaeological remains and relics of various dynasties, incluDing settlement archaeology. RegarDing this, we have already mentioned in the introduction of prehistoric settlement sites in the previous chapter.

Although the Qin-Han period settlement sites seen in Henan are not as rich as prehistoric society, there are still many Discoveries, among which there is no lack of settlements with village nature.

A joint survey team of the Henan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology and the Department of Archaeology of Wuhan University, between October 2006 and February 2007, conducted an archaeological survey of 200 square kilometers around Huangtucheng and its surrounDing area in Huaibin County, Henan, Discovering a total of 76 sites from the Neolithic to Han dynasty.

Except for 5 cemeteries, 71 should be settlement sites, among which 41 contain Han dynasty cultural factors or Han dynasty remains. The area where these Han dynasty sites are densely Distributed is also the area where modern villages are dense, mainly located on the east bank of the Lü River and the south bank of its tributaries.

Geographically, Huaibin County is located in the middle and upper reaches of the Huai River, under Xinyang city, Henan Province. Huangtucheng and its surrounDing area are located at the southern end of the Huang-Huai Plain, with fertile land suitable for agricultural production.

From the fact that the Distribution positions of Han dynasty settlements are roughly close to modern villages, combined with production tools such as stone axes, stone sickles, stone adzes, pottery beaters, and pottery spinning wheels Discovered in the survey, these settlement sites cannot be ruled out as agricultural villages.

Among the Qin-Han settlement sites excavated archaeologically in Henan, the more typical ones are the Xiaozhai Site in Suiping and the Sanyangzhuang Han dynasty settlement site in Neihuang, Henan. Two important sites are selected for introduction as follows.

The Xiaozhai Site, located west of Xiaozhai village, Zhushi township, about 13 kilometers southwest of Suiping County, Henan Province, on the east bank of the Sha River. The site is 400 meters long from east to west and 300 meters wide from north to south, covering an area of about 120,000 square meters.

The usage period of the settlement site is from the late Warring states to the Eastern Han dynasty, dominated by the Western Han period. The site cleared 8 roads and 28 wells, with no residential remains Discovered.

Except for 4 roads in the northwest with unclear periods, the other 4 roads should belong to Han dynasty roads, arranged orderly in east-west and north-south Directions.

Two are best preserved, of which one road is 144 meters long and 5.5-7.5 meters wide, running through the middle of the site; the other is 210 meters long and 14 meters wide, intersecting with the previous east-west road at a T-junction in the middle of the site, together forming the main road of the site.

Archaeological reports show that the former road was repaired in the Eastern Han period, inDicating that the site was used at least until the Eastern Han period. Flat tiles with interior cloth patterns and fragments of pottery such as basins and jars were found mixed in the road.

The wells include 16 pottery-ring wells, 5 brick-arch wells, and 7 earthen wells, among which earthen wells were used earliest, pottery wells second, and brick wells latest.

They are regularly arranged in six east-west rows, Distributed parallel along the east-west Direction, with a very dense layout, and the nearest Distance between wells is only 7 meters.

Among the earthen wells, not only builDing materials such as flat tiles, tube tiles, and bricks were cleared, but also pottery daily utensils such as pottery funnels, jars, basins, urns, and bowls, stone tools such as stone Discs and grinDing stones, as well as copper ear spoons were Discovered.

Although no residential sites were found at the Xiaozhai Site, from the orderly arrangement of roads and wells, and the large number of unearthed relics such as architectural components and pottery, this should have been a settlement site.

Some scholars pointed out that "this site may have had residents living in a planned, relatively orderly, and concentrated manner from the late Warring states period, and this relatively concentrated residence method continued until the Eastern Han," and further believed that "this may be related to the li residence method recorded in documents and bamboo and silk records." Although the statement of "li residence" is not conclusive, it is reasonable to speculate that it was a concentrated settlement.

The Sanyangzhuang Site, located north of Sanyangzhuang, Liangzhuang Town, Neihuang County, Henan Province, about 30 kilometers north of Neihuang County seat, and about 45 kilometers southeast of the current Yellow River channel, is located in the old Yellow River channel in southern Neihuang County, with undulating sand dunes on the surface, and the Han dynasty cultural layer and remains averaging about 4.5 meters below the current surface.

Within the 1,500-meter-long Xiao River channel range, 4 relatively large-area Han dynasty architectural remains were Discovered, inDicating that this should have been a relatively large-scale settlement site in the Han dynasty, and very likely had several settlement areas, each containing several courtyards.

From the remains and relics, Sanyangzhuang is a typical agricultural village site.

The first courtyard remains, with an area of about 1,800 square meters and a cleared area of more than 400 square meters, should be the main house part, incluDing courtyard foundation, house foundation, tile roof, rammed earth wall, and mud-mixing pool, as well as unused tiles, construction waste accumulation, stoves, and ash pits.

The courtyard foundation is about 20 meters long from north to south and 18 meters wide from east to west, about 0.3 meters higher than the surrounDing ground; the house foundation and tile roof are located in the western part of the courtyard foundation, possibly a house facing east from west, with two bays; the southern bay is about 4.5 meters wide from north to south and within 6 meters long from east to west; the northern bay is wider than the southern one, about 5.7 meters wide from north to south, with rammed earth walls on the east and west, about 65 cm thick, with existing height of 50-65 cm.

The tile roof can be Divided into two parts, respectively located at the north and south ends of the house foundation; the southern part is northwest-southeast oriented, with the tile roof high in the north and low in the south, still sloped, with the upward-laying of flat tiles and the covering of tube tiles preserving their original appearance; the northern tile roof is east-west oriented, high in the south and low in the north, still sloped, with the structure of flat tiles and tube tiles clear.

In the northeast corner of the courtyard foundation, a large area of broken tiles, bricks, and pottery fragments was cleared, mixed with inDividual iron tools. Around the house foundation, some pottery fragments were also found, such as basins, jars, urns, and water troughs, as well as small iron tools unearthed.

In the southern part of the excavated area, 1 well belonging to the courtyard composition was Discovered. South of the well, there is 1 east-west Han dynasty road, about 4 meters wide.

The Shaojiagou Site, located in the northern suburb of Gaoyou city, jiangsu, on the east bank of Gaoyou Lake. The existing area of the site is 750-850 square meters, with cliffs at the northern edge, sloping slopes on the east and south sides, and the west side relatively well preserved, with an excavation area of 400 square meters.

It cleared 2 pottery-ring wells, 1 storage pit, 2 ash pits, 2 ash Ditches, and 2 wooden-coffin tombs, with 387 relics unearthed. The site period is the late Eastern Han dynasty.

Among the unearthed relics, pottery is the most numerous, with 323 pieces, of which daily utensils include 33 jars, 9 pots, 20 "lamp-shaped" vessels, 34 basins, 1 dou, 2 three-legged basins, 131 bowls, 6 bowls, 3 yu vessels, 3 steamers, 16 lamp Dishes, 1 min vessel, 5 "arc-shaped" vessels, 1 vat, and 3 pottery lids; production tools include 8 spinning wheels and 8 net sinkers; architectural components include 3 bricks, 12 tiles and tile ends, etc.; there are more than 10 vessels of unclear attribute.

There are 19 porcelain pieces incluDing jars, pots, and yu vessels. Lacquerware includes 2 ear cups, 1 bowl, and 11 pieces of residual lacquer fragments. In adDition, there are agricultural production tools such as iron plows, iron hammers, and bamboo washing baskets, with the iron plow still having a wooden handle connection when Discovered.

Others include whetstones, copper coins, bamboo mats, straw mats, straw sandal soles, peach pits, melon seeds, and cattle, dog, and fish bones. The site also unearthed talisman wooden slips, "Heavenly Emperor Messenger" sealing clay, and red-ink inscriptions on pottery pots, which should be Daoist relics.

Although no remains such as houses or roads were seen in the above excavation situation, from the cleared remains such as ash pits, ash Ditches, wells, tombs, and human skeletons, Shaojiagou should have been a settlement in the Eastern Han period.

Moreover, the more than 300 daily utensils and agricultural production tools such as iron plows, iron hammers, and bamboo washing baskets further inDicate that this was a village site with very strong life atmosphere and agricultural nature.

The Daoist relics among the remains inDicate that Daoism in the Eastern Han period had not only been deified but also widely penetrated into folk society.

The Xiaoshancun Site, located at Xiaoshancun village, Fenghuang Town, Zhangjiagang city, jiangsu, on the east side of Heyang Mountain.

The site surface is mainly farmland, with rivers, canals, and ponds interspersed, overall trenDing southwest-northeast, about 300 meters long and 100 meters wide, with a total area of about 27,000 square meters and an excavation area of 808 square meters.

The site is dominated by cultural remains from the Han to Three Kingdoms periods, clearing 1 well, 10 ash pits, 4 ash Ditches, and 2 tombs. The well is circular, with a Diameter of 1 meter and depth of 1.75 meters.

The ash pits are all sloping-wall pits, with round or nearly flat bottoms, having three shapes: circular pits, irregular circular pits, and square pits.

A large number of architectural components such as flat tiles and tube tiles, and fragments of pottery vessels such as Ding tripods, pots, jars, basins, and steamers were unearthed in the ash Ditches and ash pits. The unearthed relics mainly include brick and tile fragments, pottery, and a small amount of porcelain and stone tools.

Among them, architectural components are the most numerous, with 1,009 flat tiles, mostly gray-blue, a few redDish, with combined cord and string patterns on the outer wall, and various inner walls incluDing plain, cloth, nipple, square, and Diamond patterns, plus 14 tile ends, 14 hollow bricks, and 259 tube tiles.

There are 601 restored pottery pieces, incluDing 579 clay pottery and 22 hard pottery, with vessel types mainly being daily utensils such as Ding tripods, pots, jars, basins, and steamers, and production tools such as net cones, spinning wheels, and pottery Discs.

From the remains such as wells, ash pits, ash Ditches, and tombs Discovered at the Xiaoshancun Site, as well as the rich unearthed relics, this place had strong traces of human life from the Han to Three Kingdoms periods, and should be a settlement site, especially the excavation of a large number of architectural components such as bricks and tiles further inDicates this point.

(5) village Sites in Other Regions

In adDition to the relatively typical Qin-Han period village sites in the above regions, archaeological excavations across the country have also Discovered Qin-Han period settlement sites or sites containing Qin-Han cultural factors, but they are often overlooked due to small excavation areas or unclear village nature.

The following introduces sites with prominent village attributes and typical characteristics.

The Liuwei Site, located east of Liuwei village, Changgou Town, Sixian County, Anhui, on the north bank of the current Bian River. The site is 500 meters long from north to south and 250 meters wide from east to west, with a total area of more than 10,000 square meters. It was excavated twice successively, with a cleared area of 1,600 square meters.

The cultural remains are dominated by Tang-Song, and Han dynasty remains and relics are also very rich. The Han dynasty remains are mainly Distributed in the north-central position, with 7 wells, 7 water Ditches, 10 ash pits, and 1 tomb.

The wells have two types: brick wells and earthen wells, both circular, with most well Diameters of 1-1.5 meters and residual depths of 1-2.5 meters, with a small amount of Han dynasty pottery fragments unearthed in the wells. Except for two irregular-shaped water Ditches, the rest are elongated, should be Han dynasty living drainage facilities.

The ash pits unearthed a large number of Han dynasty relics, incluDing cord-pattern red pottery flat tiles, tube tiles, and tile end fragments, and also found daily utensils such as bowls, boxes, plates, dou, pots, urns, vats, and jars, as well as pottery production tools such as spinning wheels and pottery Discs, and iron farm tools such as iron shovels, iron spades, iron plows, iron chisels, and iron rake teeth.

A large number of living utensils and architectural components inDicate that this should have been a Han dynasty living residential area. iron farm tools, textile tools, and remains such as wells both inDicate that the Liuwei Site belongs to an agricultural settlement site and reflect the progress of Han dynasty agricultural technology.

One kilometer northeast of the Liuwei Site is Yangchenghu Lake. Based on relevant records in "Guangxu Sihong Hezhi," the archaeological report speculates whether Yangchenghu Lake is the old site of Hong County county seat in the Han dynasty remains to be proven by further archaeological work.

About 7.5 meters south of the site near the current Bian River estuary, remains of the Bian River embankment from the Tang-Song period were Discovered.

The Sandaohao Site, located at Sandaohao village, 1.5 kilometers north of Liaoyang city, Liaoning, in the alluvial plain on the west bank of the Taizi River, covering an area of about 4 square kilometers, with an excavation area of more than 10,000 square meters.

It Discovered 6 residential sites, 11 wells, 7 brick kiln sites, 2 sections of stone-paved roads, and 368 children's urn-coffin tombs, with a total of more than 190,000 relics incluDing pottery and tile fragments. The cultural accumulation of the Sandaohao Site has good continuity and consistent nature.

Although each architectural site is mostly Divided into upper and lower two or three layers, they should be early and late remains of the same culture. The Distance between the 6 residential courtyards is 15 meters for the nearest and about 30 meters or more for the farthest.

Courtyards are generally composed of houses, stoves, earthen cellars, wells, toilet earthen Ditches, and wooden fence livestock pens. In the middle and near the courtyard sites, brick kiln sites and cobblestone roads are Distributed.

The first residential site, about 20 meters long from east to west and 13 meters wide from north to south. The site cleared 1 loess house foundation and 1 circular builDing, the latter located at the east end of the former.

Three stove sites of Different sizes were found in the residential site; 1 small earthen cellar, more than 60 cm deep, unearthed iron tools, bricks, and pottery fragments.

12-13 meters west of the house foundation is 1 pottery-tube well, with 18 sections of pottery tubes, 4.5 meters deep; "small Banliang coins," iron tools, pottery fragments, and brick kiln slag were unearthed in the well.

In adDition, many relics were found in the house site and lower ash layer, incluDing bronze tools such as sword guards, belt hooks, arrowheads, knife coins, small Banliang, Wuzhu, and Dabu Huangqian, and iron tools such as hoes, sickles, residual cart axles, arrowheads, knives, awls, and pot fragments, as well as pottery vessels such as jars, basins, steamers, dou, pots, spinning wheels, and tile ends, and also saw a small pile of sorghum carbonized by burning.

The second residential site, 38 meters long from east to west and about 15 meters wide from north to south. The site has three successive architectural remains superimposed.

The early site is westward, with only a section of ash layer containing tiles and pottery fragments, with 1 earthen cellar well at its west end; 1 small stove site at the east end, with one-knife small round coins, large Banliang coins, and small Banliang coins found; Wuzhu coins were found in the upper part of the well.

The middle residential site is eastward, preserving 1 section of loess platform, with a large number of relics such as tiles and pottery fragments Distributed, possibly a small house with earthen walls, wooden columns, and grass-tile roofs.

There is 1 livestock pen at the west end of the house site, enclosed by 6 square wooden columns, with the pit full of feces and grass and ash; 3 oval column holes remain behind the livestock pen, possibly remains of fences or similar.

There is 1 earthen cellar well to the west, with the well full of ash soil, a stone-supported stove site found in the upper part, and 1 horse skeleton found slightly lower. The late house site is in the middle, with 6 column plinths remaining, and the room area may not be large. This builDing is close to brick kilns No.

1 and 2, seemingly related to them. There is 1 earthen cellar well behind the house site, with the well full of burnt broken bricks.

Slightly farther east is 1 ash pit, unearthed Wang Mang's coin "Daquan Wushi." The relics seen at the second residential site include bronze tools such as arrowheads, belt hooks, buttons, and finger rings, iron tools such as plowshares, hoes, adzes, spades, shovels, sickles, arrowheads, belt hooks, swords, knives, awls, and sha spears, and pottery such as mills, pots, spinning wheels, bowls, jars, basins, steamers, and pots.

The third residential site, 34 meters long from east to west and about 18 meters wide from north to south, well preserved. The upper late residential site only has several cobblestone piles of Different sizes, plinths, tiles, and pottery fragments remaining.

The lower layer has 1 loess house site, with a square livestock pen at the west end of the house site, enclosed by 12 square wooden columns, with livestock feces and rotten grass in the pen. There is a toilet behind the livestock pen. Not far to the right front of the livestock pen are 2 earthen cellars of Different sizes.

Not far west of the house site are 2 earthen cellar wells, one of which has a cobblestone pile of a late builDing, and the other earthen cellar well is a square-wood wall well, possibly for production water. The unearthed relics are equivalent to the above.

The fourth residential site, about 30 meters long from east to west and 16 meters wide from north to south. The upper late builDing only has 1 square cobblestone pile remaining. The lower layer has 1 loess platform house site.

There is a 6-meter-long square livestock pen at the west end of the house site, enclosed by 14 square wooden columns, with a pen door left in the south, and livestock feces and ash soil in the pen. There is a toilet behind the livestock pen. There is 1 small earthen cellar in the house courtyard.

There is 1 large earthen cellar behind the house site on the left and right, more than 2 meters deep. More than 20 meters in front left of the house site is 1 pottery-tube well, with two human skeletons, one male and one female, found superimposed more than 1 meter below the well mouth, with 2 copper finger rings on the female finger bones.

Unearthed bronze tools include arrowheads, hairpins, belt hooks, mirror fragments, and bronze vessel fragments; iron tools include hoes, adzes, spades, shovels, sickles, cart axle fragments, chisels, drill bits, knives, awls, and pot fragments; ornaments include glass, stone, agate, and bead ornaments; pottery includes steamers, jars, pots, basins, and dou.

Also saw Han dynasty coins same as above.

The fifth residential site, about 30 meters long from east to west and 18 meters wide from north to south, is a well-preserved architectural site with a long residence time. The thickest part of the cultural accumulation layer is about 1.05 meters.

The upper layer at the east end of the site has paving stones, tube tiles, flat tiles, and tile ends of a Balhae kingdom builDing. The site has 1 loess platform house foundation, with a wide red-burnt earth surface Distributed on the east end floor inside the house, with square and round stove remains. There is 1 small earthen cellar to the west.

Not far east of the house is a large livestock pen, enclosed by 11 square wooden columns, about 6 meters wide. There is 1 large earthen cellar behind the pen, and a toilet to the west of the pen. There is 1 earthen cellar in the west behind the house site.

There is 1 earthen cellar well in the east, with river cobblestones filled outside the wooden well wall. About 15 meters west of the site, there is a pottery-tube well, 6 meters deep. The unearthed relics are roughly equivalent to the above residential sites.

The sixth residential site, about 22 meters wide from east to west and 30 meters long from north to south, may include three Different architectural sites. The upper residential site is incompletely preserved with fewer relics.

The northern residential site has 1 section of loess platform foundation, with tiles, pottery fragments, and column plinths Distributed on the platform. There is 1 circular earthen cellar west of the house site. There is 1 pottery-tube well, more than 4 meters deep.

The middle residential site has the same stratigraphic level, with only 1 loess platform remaining, unearthed some iron farm tools. The southern residential site has a higher stratigraphic level, with 1 loess house foundation remaining, about 3 rooms, with the west earthen wall foundation and 2 column plinths on the back wall line well preserved.

There is 1 small livestock pen at the west end of the house site, enclosed by 4 square wooden columns, about 2.05 meters wide on each side, with chaff in the accumulation, possibly a pig pen. There is a toilet behind the livestock pen.

Unearthed iron tools include small iron plowshares, shovels, hoes, adzes, sickles, cart axles, knives, awls, daggers, and pot fragments; unearthed pottery, ornaments, and coins are roughly the same as above.

There is a stone-paved main road in the village site, located north of the residential sites, trenDing from west to east then slightly south, with a total length of 166 meters, with 44 meters at the west end unexcavated, road surface about 7 meters wide, all paved with river cobblestones in three or four layers, about 35 cm thick.

There are no architectural traces such as Ditches, ridge edges, or side roads on both sides of the road. Relics similar to the above residential sites were also found on the road. There are obvious wheel ruts on the road surface, generally two parallel rows of large cart ruts.

The above about the residential situation of the Sandaohao Site is only part of the settlement site, and it is still Difficult to glimpse the overall layout of the village.

Combined with the currently archaeologically seen remains, it can be affirmed that the Sandaohao Site should belong to a Western Han dynasty village, with a long duration, used at least from the mid-Western Han to the late Western Han, and the abandonment time may be in the Xin Mang period.

From the layout, the 6 residential sites seen at the site are not connected to each other, scattered and arranged without regularity, with pottery kilns in between. Each residential site generally opens doors to the south or slightly east or west.

Except for the first residential site having no livestock pen, the basic configuration of each residential site is living space, courtyard, well, toilet, livestock pen, and cellar. Among the excavated and cleared remains, there are a large number of iron farm tools and pottery tools.

Combined with builDings such as livestock pens, it can be judged that the Sandaohao Site should be a Han dynasty village site in Northeast China.

Moreover, from the abandoned kiln sites, more than 190,000 pottery and tile fragments and a large number of farm tools, and the situation of every household having a livestock pen, this village belongs to a settlement site with agriculture, hanDicrafts, and livestock industry.

As for some scholars claiming it also has "tuntian (military agricultural colony) or garrison nature," the seen remains are insufficient to prove this point.

The Lijiaba Site, located at Qingshu village, Gaoyang Town, Yunyang County, Chongqing, on the terrace on the left bank of the Pengxi River, a tributary on the north side of the Yangtze River in the Three Gorges Reservoir area, is an ancient cultural site in the inundated area of the Three Gorges Reservoir.

Two small gullies in the middle of the terrace where the site is located Divide the terrace into three parts, which can be Divided into Shangba, Zhongba, and Xiaba from east to west.

The site is Distributed in Shangba, backed by mountains and facing the river, with an existing area of about 120,000 square meters and a core area of about 30,000 square meters. The cultural remains are dominated by the Shang-Zhou to Han, Wei, and Six Dynasties, extenDing down to the Tang-Song to Ming-Qing periods, with a long duration.

Since 1997, four large-scale excavations have been carried out here successively, with a total excavation area of 5,000 square meters, Discovering more than 50 house sites, nearly 400 tombs, and hundreds of remains such as ash pits, ash Ditches, and roads from the Eastern Zhou to the Six Dynasties.

To facilitate understanDing of the space and changes of the Lijiaba settlement, archaeological excavators Divided the residential sites of the Qin-Han and Six Dynasties periods into four phases.

The settlement Did not form a village society dominated by a certain clan, and the various surnames seen on the pottery inscriptions can corroborate this to a certain extent. A large number of cultural remains also show that Lijiaba was strongly influenced by multiple cultures incluDing the Ba-Shu culture, Chu culture, Qin culture, and Yue culture.

The unique cultural characteristics also fully demonstrate that Lijiaba was not a closed village in the traDitional sense. Therefore, its possibility as a commercial settlement in rural areas is relatively large.

The DaDitou Site, located at Dayao village, Dashu Town, Hanyuan County, Ya'an city, Sichuan, on the slope on the south bank of the Dadu River and the northern foot of Huaguo Mountain. The excavation area is 642 square meters, containing cultural accumulations of the late Neolithic, Han, Tang-Song, and Ming-Qing periods.

Among them, Han dynasty remains Discovered include 12 house foundations, 4 ash pits, 2 tombs, and 1 well. The house foundations are all single-room wattle-and-daub style, rectangular in plane. F3 has about 10 square meters of living surface, 1 fire pit, and 2 post holes.

The living surface is about 5 cm thick, baked and relatively hard; the fire pit is located in the center of the house, nearly circular in plane, about 1.55 meters in Diameter; in the center of the fire pit there is a nearly rectangular block stone about 20 cm long and 13 cm wide, surrounded by three smaller block stones.

F7 has a facade width of 4.1 meters, with two bays of depth, respectively 3.25 meters and 2.75 meters, total length 6 meters; the living surface is about 2 cm thick, relatively hard; adjacent to the south side of the house is 1 ash Ditch, possibly the house's drainage Ditch, about 3 meters wide, visible length about 10 meters, depth 0.45 meters.

F8 faces northeast, with 7 large post holes and 7 small post holes, the house should have a double-slope roof; facade width 1 bay, not less than 3.5 meters, depth 1.8-2.6 meters; there is a row of eave columns in front and behind the house; 1 ash Ditch was found to the north, a drainage Ditch, 5.5 meters long, 0.25-0.3 meters wide, 0.06 meters deep.

F27 has a residual length of 5.4 meters and residual width of 4.9 meters, with only living surface, 2 post holes, and 1 fire pit found in plane; the living surface is made of yellow sandy soil mixed with gravel and beaten, relatively hard; the fire pit is located in the north center, oval, with charcoal ash accumulated inside.

The well is circular, with a Diameter of 0.7 meters and depth of 3.4 meters. The site unearthed relics such as pottery jars, bronze mirrors, Banliang coins, iron helmets, and agate beads.

The overall layout of the DaDitou Site shows no obvious planning, no obvious road traces or remains such as enclosing walls, and no agricultural production tools were found among the seen relics, so it may not be an agricultural settlement.

The archaeological report believes that the site dates to the Western Han period and is located at the throat of the ancient "Southern Silk Road," possibly having a certain relationship with the "Southern Silk Road." Therefore, it is speculated that the possibility of the DaDitou Site being a transportation-type settlement site serving commercial exchanges cannot be ruled out.

RegarDing this, further archaeological data remains to be confirmed.

The above settlement sites are Distributed in various regions across the country, all having certain representativeness and typicality of era types, all reflecting the characteristic of adapting to local conDitions.

But overall, their scales are relatively small, and their natures and contents are also Different, some dominated by agriculture, some combining hanDicrafts and commerce, or being pure transportation-type settlements, to name a few. Overall, the site selection of these village sites Differs in Different periods and regions.

In adDition to being influenced by Different geographical conDitions, this may be closely related to Differences in population density, social historical background, and humanistic and geographical environment.

II. Scale and Formal Characteristics of Qin-Han villages

Generally speaking, villages can be Divided into two forms in terms of form: clustered villages and scattered villages. The former is the village we usually understand, formed by many residential builDings gathered together to form an obvious clustered form, with varying scales.

Measured by household number and population, large ones have hundreds of households and thousands of people, meDium ones dozens of households and hundreds of people, small ones several households and dozens of people.

The overall characteristic of clustered villages is dense residence, with roads connecting each other, streams, ponds, or other public builDings as markers or bonds, forming the aggregative characteristic of villages.

The latter is also called scattered residence form, with houses sporaDically Distributed, less obvious aggregation than the former, generally near farmland, mountains, forests, rivers, and lakes. There is no obvious dependency relationship between houses, and some scattered villages are even independent farmhouses of only one household.

Essentially, the key to Distinguishing the two is not the amount of population and the size of spatial scale, but the tightness of the interdependent relationship between houses and between houses and fields, mountains, forests, rivers, and lakes. The tendency of aggregation and Dispersion is the key element for judging the two.

As the French human geographer Albert Demangeon said in his article "rural Residential Forms": "In the landscape of a village (clustered village), houses are clustered together, which somewhat strengthens the sense of loneliness on the cultivated land; the village and its land seem to be sharply separated.

In the landscape of scattered residence, houses are not far from cultivated land, and the attraction between houses is far less than the attraction between houses and fields. Farmsteads and their management builDings are all built near the fields, and around each cultivated land, there are often walls, fences, or Ditches.

Even those small house groups called hamlets (hameau, Weiler, hamlet) seem to generally be regarded as a form of scattered residence, because they almost always mean that houses and fields are close." In terms of village connotation, clustered villages are undoubtedly the typical form of villages and the main object of Discussion, while scattered villages or scattered residence forms are often overlooked due to insufficient representativeness.

In fact, in the Discussion of village history, both should and must be included in the research perspective, because only in this way can research truly reflect the generation and development of villages.

Although these stuDies may reflect only the village form of a certain historical stage, or embody the characteristics of villages in a certain historical stage and a certain region, from deeper research results, it is entirely possible for us to glimpse that villages present Different appearances and structures in Different societies during their generation and development, and thereby reflect certain relationships between the state and local society.

(1) Scale of Qin-Han villages

The scale of a village refers to the size of its external form and the amount of its internal population, etc.

It is an important factor for measuring the population quantity, economic level, and cultural landscape of local society, and also a key prerequisite for understanDing the constituent elements, structure and layout, and residential builDing forms and structures of villages.

Therefore, it is necessary to sort out the scale of villages in the Qin-Han period. Although the relevant literature and archaeological materials are relatively scarce, from the limited materials, some speculations with historical and material evidence can still be roughly made.

1. Population Scale of villages

The population scale of a village refers to the Distribution and existence state of population in regional space within a certain period.

In a general sense, there are two ways of understanDing the Distribution state of population: first, the state's statistics on households, with strong administrative significance, reflecting the population scale and Distribution within administrative establishment units; second, the actual existence state and geographical Distribution of households.

Due to Different types of residential areas and regional environments, their population scales vary. For example, mountainous areas, plains, city walls, and villages, especially villages as natural settlements, their natural population growth or reduction is even more Difficult for the state to control and count.

Population scholars have conducted statistics on the population Distribution in the Western Han period, finDing that the population Distribution at that time was extremely uneven.

For example, the current Henan region had a population of 12.98 million, accounting for more than 22% of the national population, while its land area was only 1.74% of the Han dynasty national land area, equivalent to 77.7 people per square kilometer.

Except for Shandong, Hebei, Sichuan, Anhui, Shaanxi, jiangsu, Shanxi, etc., the population of the remaining regions was mostly below 2 million, some even less than 1 million. For this reason, it is Difficult to accurately judge the population scale of villages.

Here, the author combines documentary records and archaeological Discoveries to make a rough estimate of the population scale of Qin-Han villages.

There is no Direct expression in the literature regarDing the number of village households, but as mentioned earlier, the Han dynasty showed the phenomenon of "li-settlement unity," with the state striving to set one settlement per li at the national level.

Although there may be exceptions in vast rural areas, it at least shows that the possibility of "li" as an administrative establishment unit and "ju" as a natural settlement being equivalent in scale and household number. We might as well take "li" as a breakthrough for a brief Discussion.

"Han Shu - Chao Cuo Zhuan" says: "Make five families form a wu, wu has a chief; ten chiefs form one li." AccorDing to this understanDing, roughly 5 households are organized into one wu, and 50 households form one li.

"Gongyang Zhuan - Duke Xuan, Year 15" Eastern Han He Xiu annotation says: "One li has 80 households, eight families share one alley." Meaning 80 households form one li, 8 families share one alley.

"Hou Han Shu - Bai Guan V" says: "Li has li kui (ward chief), people have shi-wu, good and evil are reported." Original annotation says: "Li kui manages one li of 100 households. Shi manages 10 families, wu manages 5 families, to mutually inspect." Here "li" has 100 households.

These documents have Different expressions on the number of households in "li," with large gaps. The occurrence of this situation is related to residential type, region, and time.

First, in economically developed Central Plains regions such as Henan, population density is very high, and whether it is "li" or natural settlement villages, the possibility of more households is greater, conversely, the possibility of fewer households is greater.

Second, the number of people resiDing in city walls is relatively concentrated, and the number of households in li is relatively more, while in rural areas, with vast land and sparse population, the number of households in "li" or villages is correspondingly less.

Finally, the population of a country or region will increase or decrease at Different stages due to various reasons, which is a very normal situation, but will also affect documentary records.

Under normal circumstances, the number of households in li or ju is between several households and dozens of households. Among the 41 li in the "Garrison Map" unearthed from Han Tomb No. 3 at Mawangdui in Changsha, 16 li have confirmable household numbers, with uneven household counts.

Among them, Shangshe li has 23 households, Zi li 30 households, He li 53 households, Zi li 13 households, Lü li 35 households, Bo li 17 households, Sha li 43 households, Zhi li 68 households, Chengyang li 17 households, Yuan li 81 households, Ci li 35 households, Lu li 43 households, Jing li 57 households, Zi li 12 households, Long li 108 households, Shexia li 47 households.

Among the above household numbers, Long li is the li with the most households in the "Garrison Map," followed by Yuan li and Zhi li, fewer such as Bo li and Zi li, others mostly around 40 households. The average household number in the "Garrison Map" is between 40-50 households. AccorDing to bamboo slips from Han Tomb No.

10 at Fenghuang Mountain in jiangling, Hubei, the Zheng Li granary register records only 25 households. If adDing people who Did not borrow grain, the possibility of the household number being around 30 is relatively large.

"Han Shu - Zhang Anshi Zhuan" also records: "(Emperor Xuan) then issued an eDict: 'Establish 30 families to guard the tomb for the former Ye Ting Ling Zhang He.' The emperor personally arranged their li, resiDing west of the house, south of the cockfighting old man's house." The state-level establishment of "li" also basically takes 30 households as the scale.

This household situation, especially the household numbers seen in the "Garrison Map," although reflecting the household scale of settlements in the southern Han dynasty region, also has certain explanatory power for villages in rural areas across the country in the Han dynasty. Han dynasty villages may generally have around 40 households.

Documentary records show that there are also many Han dynasty settlements with hundreds or even hundreds of households. "Yinwan Han Tomb Bamboo Slips" records Donghai Commandery "counties 170, li 2,534," "households 266,290+." If calculated accorDingly, average one li is about 105 households, among which large ones reach hundreds or more.

"Han Shu - Wu Wuzi Zhuan" records that after Emperor Xuan of Han ascended the throne, in the first year of Benshi (73 BCE), he posthumously titled his grandfather Crown Prince Li Liu Ju, saying: "'The late crown prince is posthumously titled Li, establish 200 families for offering yi.

Shi LiangDi is titled Lady Li, establish 30 families to guard the tomb. The garden establishes zhang and cheng, with weekly guards and offerings accorDing to law.' Use Xieli ju of Wenxiang, Hu County as Li Garden." From this, the guarDians of Li Garden may be over 200 households. Another example, "Juyan Xin jian" records: "...

counties, xiang, ju transfer and move official households (E.P.T40:46)." "Ting chiefs 21 people, received 3 people from Lecheng Marquisate, total 24 people. All below ting 50 people, received 4 people from Lecheng Marquisate, fixed below chief officials 54 people.

Xiang 8, ju 44, households 7,984, mouths 15,735 (E.P.T50:3)." These two bamboo slip documents both record the quota allocation of ting and marquisate officials in the Han dynasty, and also record the household situation of 44 ju and the number of conscriptable solDiers.

AccorDing to the bamboo slip record of "xiang 8, ju 44, households 7,984, mouths 15,735," 8 xiang and 44 ju, total 7,984 households, can conscript 15,735 solDiers, that is, average 2 people per household perform military service. Also accorDing to 44 ju, each ju 181.5 households, if each household about 5 people, then population is over 900.

In adDition to li-ju of 100 or hundreds of households, there are also large settlements of 1,000 households.

"Han Shu - Shi Dan Zhuan" records: after Emperor Cheng of Western Han ascended the throne, "enfeoff Dan as Wuyang Marquis, state WuQiang ju of Tan in Donghai, 1,100 households." WuQiang ju is obviously a giant settlement, not a village in the strict sense, but on the contrary may belong to the location of a county or xiang government seat.

Such large ju may be Divided into several li or small ju accorDing to the number of households. In the late Eastern Han, there were also phenomena of 1,000-household settlements. For example, during Dong Zhuo's rebellion, "Rong Rong at that time led over 1,000 families of clansmen, taking refuge in the western mountains of Mi.

(Xun) Yu said to the elders: 'Yingchuan is a land of four battles. If the world changes...'" "Sanguozhi" records: Tian Chou also "led all his clansmen and other followers of several hundred people... then entered Xuwu Mountain, built a residence in a deep, dangerous, and flat place, personally farmed to support his parents.

Common people returned to him, reaching over 5,000 households in a few years." Han Rong leaDing "over 1,000 families" of clansmen to take refuge in the mountains, and Tian Chou leaDing clansmen of "several hundred people" into Xuwu Mountain, although not necessarily villages, in connection with the wu bao (fortified settlements) with military self-defense nature in the Wei-Jin-Northern and Southern Dynasties, should have the meaning of mountain settlements.

In summary, villages in the Qin-Han period, in terms of population scale, may generally be 30-50 households, a few over 100 households, and 1,000 or more households also existed, and this should only occur under extremely special circumstances such as turbulent situations.

In adDition, it needs to be pointed out that the population number of various settlements incluDing villages is not fixed and unchanging, but dynamic: in periods of social stability and economic prosperity, it may expand; in periods of social turmoil and people's livelihood being destitute, it may shrink.

In general circumstances and significance, with population growth, villages will change, either expanDing scale or deriving new villages, because when the land in a certain regional area is insufficient to meet the growing population, new land can only be opened up elsewhere.

Of course, there is also population migration, which will also lead to the growth or reduction of village population scale, etc. Such examples are numerous.

2. Spatial Scale of villages

The spatial scale of a village refers to the size and presentation state of the area occupied by the village within a certain regional space. What exactly was the spatial scale of villages in the Qin-Han period? Although it is Difficult to know from documentary records, fortunately, archaeologically excavated village sites provide us with physical samples for understanDing.

The above introduced the survey situation of Han dynasty settlement sites in the Huangtucheng area of Huaibin County, Henan. Within 200 square kilometers, a total of 76 remains from the Neolithic to Han dynasty were Discovered.

ExcluDing 5 cemeteries, there are still 71 settlement sites, among which 41 contain Han dynasty or are purely Han dynasty remains.

Except for 1 with unknown area, accorDing to area size, these settlements can be Divided into 4 grades from large to small: the largest sites are 2, with areas of 285,000-301,000 square meters; meDium sites are 3, with areas of 67,000-91,000 square meters; small-meDium sites are 14, with areas of 10,000-49,000 square meters; those below 10,000 square meters are small sites, 21 in number.

Among them, the larger Huangtucheng Site and Zhaozhuang Site, used from the early Yangshao to the Han dynasty, although no city wall remains were seen, the possibility that they belonged to regional settlement centers such as county yi or xiang in the Han dynasty cannot be ruled out.

The remaining area settlements may绝大多数 be orDinary villages, with the largest no more than 91,000 square meters, generally below 50,000 square meters, and small sites with areas around 3,000 square meters being the most numerous and common. In terms of quantity, orDinary settlements below 50,000 square meters account for 85%.

Moreover, the number of houses in small sites is also very small.

These statistical data, on one hand, inDicate that in the Qin-Han period, as a densely populated place, Henan's village spatial scale was generally below 50,000 square meters, especially those from several thousand to 10,000 square meters being more common; on the other hand, a large number of small settlement sites inDicate that the number of scattered villages in this period was not small, and may be a main form of early village development.
